summary: Vehicular edge computing (VEC) enables latency-sensitive applications by bringing computing and networking resources closer to vehicles. However, existing approaches often overlook network contention among co-located services with heterogeneous and dynamic latency requirements. While time-sensitive networking (TSN) provides bounded-latency communication, conventional and reinforcement learning-based schedulers struggle to adapt to highly dynamic vehicular environments and inter-queue dependencies. To address these limitations, we propose a multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) approach for queue-level scheduling in TSN-enabled VEC. Each TSN queue is assigned an autonomous agent that jointly learns the queue service order and time-slot duration to minimize deadline misses under speed-dependent latency requirements. We employ multi-agent proximal policy optimization (MAPPO) to enable coordinated yet autonomous scheduling decisions. Evaluation against single-agent, multi-agent, and non-learning-based baselines shows that MAPPO provides robust performance across different traffic profiles. Compared with centralized single-agent methods, it reduces service latency by up to 66.2% and improves reliability by up to 271.8%. Furthermore, unlike urgency-based heuristics, MAPPO ensures balanced scheduling while achieving lower inference times compared to other MARL methods.
title: Deadline-Aware Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for TSN-Based Vehicular Edge Networks

summary: Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) dispatch is beginning to move beyond isolated path planning and optimization-driven resource allocation toward system-level coordination supported by semantic reasoning and LLM-based interfaces. This survey provides a unified characterization of LLM-enabled UAV dispatch systems that bridges semantic intent, symbolic decision-making, and physical UAV execution. Rather than treating LLMs as standalone add-ons, we conceptualize them as a cross-layer semantic orchestration layer connecting human instructions, external solvers, and distributed control modules. We organize the literature into four representative dispatch paradigms: pipeline dispatch, global assignment dispatch, decentralized agentic dispatch, and divide-and-conquer dispatch. For each paradigm, we analyze its decision logic, system structure, control flow, representative methods, and potential LLM roles. We further examine how LLMs support semantic parsing, retrieval-grounded planning, solver orchestration, local agent reasoning, multi-agent coordination, safety assessment, and human-facing explanation. We discuss the implications of these paradigms for scalability, robustness, coordination burden, and verification requirements, and identify open challenges including latency-aware reasoning, grounding reliability, physical feasibility guarantees, edge deployment, privacy protection, and distributed consistency. This survey provides a system-level taxonomy and design perspective for integrating LLMs into safety-critical UAV dispatch systems.
title: LLM-Enabled UAV Dispatch: A System-Level Survey and Taxonomy

summary: Environments are the foundation of recursive self-improvement: they provide the problems agents work on and the feedback used to evaluate progress. Yet constructing challenging research environments with reliable evaluation still depends on domain experts, limiting their scale and disciplinary coverage. We introduce RSI-Forge, a multi-agent pipeline that turns published papers into executable environments for self-improvement. Three agents coordinate construction, reproduction, and review to produce tasks with automated evaluators; each paper's method is independently reimplemented to establish a baseline score. We present 210 environments across 18 fields, including 90 reviewed by independent human domain experts. Both experts and agent judges give high ratings to the potential for improving the provided starting solutions and the evaluators' ability to distinguish solution quality, whereas experts are more critical of shortcut resistance, faithfulness to the source paper, and whether a single idea can exhaust a task. To validate their use for repeated improvement, we evaluate four models over 3 successive attempts on 120 environments, with each attempt inheriting prior code and notes while model weights remain fixed. At least one model improves after the first attempt in 84% of environments. Models also outperform the reproduced paper methods in 68 of the 120 environments, demonstrating room for gains beyond these baselines. Transcript analysis identifies work beyond parameter tuning in 95% of these successful attempts. Analysis of the resulting trajectories shows that models scoring lower on these tasks explore less, more often accept gains smaller than the reported standard error, and rely more heavily on tuning to the development set. RSI-Forge provides a scalable approach to constructing research environments for training and evaluating self-improving agents.
title: RSI-Forge: From Research Papers to Environments for Recursive Self-Improvement

summary: THINKIT: workflows for SSI-assisted scientific research THINKIT is a set of coordinated workflows for using Synthetic Scientific Intelligence (SSI) in scientific research: understanding physical problems, examining literature and evidence, developing research projects and proposals, and preparing scientific manuscripts. It is intended for researchers, doctoral students, and research teams, particularly in the physical sciences and engineering. Its purpose is to make scientific interaction with SSI more disciplined, transparent, and controllable by the researcher. THINKIT provides a shared framework for clarification, reasoning, evidence assessment, and scientific decisions, reducing the need to repeatedly explain how the SSI should approach the work. Status: Validated experimental release Feedback : If you use THINKIT, I would be grateful for comments on usability, scientific workflow, and problems you encounter: Feedback link   Guiding principles Researcher-led discussion. The researcher controls the direction, depth, and pace of the work. THINKIT starts from the available observations, evidence, and ideas, asks questions when consequential ambiguities remain, and addresses the current question without automatically expanding the task. Physical understanding before calculation. Mechanisms, forcing, constraints, and relevant regimes guide the choice of equations and models. Numerical inputs and computational work serve a defined scientific purpose. Iterative hypothesis development and testing. Hypotheses are formulated, examined, refined, or rejected through checks of internal consistency and comparison with relevant literature, experiments, or numerical results. The researcher’s hypothesis is examined before alternatives are developed. Broader idea generation follows the researcher’s request or choice; evaluating an idea does not authorize replacing it. Literature integrated into reasoning. Targeted literature checks support focused research questions and consequential claims. Supporting, contradictory, and missing evidence are made explicit, together with the limits of source access. Clear evidence status. Observations, source claims, assumptions, derived results, interpretations, and provisional ideas remain distinguishable. Adopting a working hypothesis does not establish its validity, and polished wording must not imply stronger evidence than is available. What to expect from the four methods PHYSIT — physical understanding and modelling through critical discussion of the problem. Starts by identifying the main physical elements, processes, regions or regimes relevant to the question and by establishing a shared understanding of the problem. It combines existing scientific knowledge and targeted literature evidence with an iterative process of generating, testing, rejecting and refining physical hypotheses. Candidate explanations are checked for internal consistency and against available observations, data and established knowledge. When a sufficiently supported physical picture emerges, PHYSIT can develop it further into scaling relations, reduced descriptions or theoretical models. LITIT — scientific literature, evidence and terminology. Starts from a clearly defined scientific question and organizes the search around relevant phenomena, mechanisms, models, methods and neighboring fields. It identifies and screens literature, distinguishes source-stated results from interpretation, evaluates what individual sources actually support, and keeps uncertainties and source-access limitations explicit. It also collects relevant scientific terminology, definitions and usage from the inspected literature to support consistent reasoning and writing across the project. When important conclusions depend on unavailable details, LITIT identifies priority papers and may request full texts. PROPOSIT — research projects, proposals, review and revision. title: THINKIT: A plugin for user-led and user-controlled scientific development in collaboration with Synthetic Scientific Intelligence (SSI)

summary: tdfpy is a Python package for reading Bruker timsTOF data from analysis.tdf and analysis.tdf_bin files inside a .d directory. It accesses the SQLite metadata and compressed binary peak data directly, so workflows do not need the Bruker native library. High-level readers represent data-dependent acquisition, data-independent acquisition, and parallel reaction monitoring runs through frames, precursors, isolation windows, targets, and transitions. Metadata is loaded when a run is opened, while raw peak arrays are decoded only when requested. Spectrum extraction can retain ion mobility as arrays of mass-to-charge ratio, intensity, and inverse reduced mobility. Processing pipelines support region exclusion, smoothing, configurable noise filters, and two centroiding approaches: greedy peak merging in floating-point mass space and watershed region growth in time-of-flight index space. Frames and acquisition objects can also be selected by identifiers, mass-to-charge ranges, and retention time. tdfpy is intended for proteomics workflows that need scriptable access to timsTOF measurements, mobility-resolved peaks, and PASEF acquisition metadata on Linux, macOS, or Windows.
title: tdfpy: A Python package for parsing and centroiding Bruker timsTOF mass spectrometry data

summary: This work investigated the capability of multilayer perceptron artificial neural network (MLP–ANN), stochastic gradient boosting (SGB) tree, radial basis function artificial neural network (RBF–ANN), and adaptive neuro-fuzzy inference system (ANFIS) models to determine the heat capacity ( C p ) of ionanofluids in terms of the nanoparticle concentration ( x ) and the critical temperature ( T c ), operational temperature ( T ), acentric factor ( ω ), and molecular weight ( M w ) of pure ionic liquids (ILs). To this end, a comprehensive database of literature reviews was searched. The results of the SGB model were more satisfactory than the other models. Furthermore, an analysis was done to determine the outlying bad data points. It showed that most of the experimental data points were located in a reliable zone for the development of the model. The mean squared error and R 2 were 0.00249 and 0.987, 0.0132 and 0.9434, 0.0320 and 0.8754, and 0.0201 and 0.9204 for the SGB, MLP–ANN, ANFIS, and RBF–ANN, respectively. According to this study, the ability of SGB for estimating the C p of ionanofluids was shown to be greater than other models. By eliminating the need for conducting costly and time-consuming experiments, the SGB strategy showed its superiority compared with experimental measurements. Furthermore, the SGB displayed great generalizability because of the stochastic element. Therefore, it can be highly applicable to unseen conditions. Furthermore, it can help chemical engineers and chemists by providing a model with low parameters that yields satisfactory results for estimating the C p of ionanofluids. Additionally, the sensitivity analysis showed that C p is directly related to T , M w , and T c , and has an inverse relation with ω and x . M w and T c had the highest impact and ω had the lowest impact on C p .
title: Estimating the heat capacity of non-newtonian ionanofluid systems using ANN, ANFIS, and SGB tree algorithms

summary: Lean Verification for “Uniform Hiding and Two Routes to Relative Accuracy in Gaussian Boson Sampling” — Version 2.0 Version 2.0 integrates the full Lean formalizations of A1–A4 into the uniform-hiding development accompanying Hongru Zhao’s manuscript. The four scientific axioms used by version 1.3.0 are removed and replaced by proved theorem/data declarations preserving their original full contracts. The public hiding theorem, quantitative corollary, dimension ranges and constants are unchanged. The integrated proofs establish: A1 — COE principal-block law: the exact Haar principal corner law, including the boundary dimension, with its literal determinant density and self-normalization. A2 — Takagi–Weyl integration: global spectrum measurability and the flat complex-symmetric integration law, with one positive finite constant for arbitrary measurable permutation-invariant tests and measurable target spaces. The historical A2Prime name is retained for compatibility. A3 — Gaussian GSVD beta-Jacobi law: the squared generalized-singular-value law on the original real and complex Gaussian pair carriers, including global coordinate measurability and the full original dimension range. A4 — Wishart tensor moments: both direct and inverse tensor-moment formulas with the original matching-Gram coefficient convention. The supplied Wishart probability law and its transform characterization remain explicit theorem hypotheses. The all-input uniform-hiding theorem covers every 1 ≤ N,K ≤ M , including K < N , at the bound min{1, 615172 N²/M} . Its normalized and unscaled product forms, Corollary 2.2 and source-scale (S62) specialization are retained. The assembled Route 1 relative-accuracy bounds use these integrated proofs and the included companion Gaussian anticoncentration development. Lean’s standard foundations— propext , Classical.choice , and Quot.sound —remain. The executable endpoint audits require exactly that foundation set. Removing the four scientific axioms does not remove the explicit probability-model, dimension or estimator hypotheses from the theorem statements. Fresh verification passed on 8 October 2026 (America/Chicago). The named public build and two separate Lean audit executions each returned exit code zero. The exact 18 provider/public endpoints passed, and the transitive inventory audited 19,639 imported local theorem declarations across 1,162 modules , from 1,241 current Lean source files , with zero scientific axioms . The allowed logical foundations are the three listed above. The fresh build invocation reused pinned dependencies and unaffected compiled-module caches; it was not a wholly uncached check or an independent checker run. The source-linked result and command logs are recorded in verification/FINAL_VERIFICATION.json . Historical September receipts retain their original snapshot meaning. Archive hashes and fresh-extraction checks establish package integrity separately from proof validation. The photon-sector normalization, generating function, passive photon-number conservation, optimized reference scale, average-TV sampler bound, Route 1 asymptotics and all-input applications from version 1.3.0 are preserved. The squeezed-vacuum coefficients, passive tensor action and collision-free hafnian probability are adopted optical-model definitions; deriving the full model from quantum dynamics remains outside this development. Route 2 remains a conditional deduction with an explicit symmetric-Gaussian matrix-comparison premise. This release does not claim a proof of the Shou comparison or complete actual-law Route 2 assembly. The companion symmetric-Gaussian small-ball theorem is available separately. The package contains Lean sources, pinned configuration, the portable verifier, documentation, source-to-manuscript correspondence, provenance and verification records. It preserves the original version 1.3.0 archive byte-f
title: Lean Verification for "Uniform Hiding and Two Routes to Relative Accuracy in Gaussian Boson Sampling"

summary: Google Earth Engine (GEE) and Microsoft Planetary Computer (MPC) both distribute Sentinel-2 Level-2A surface reflectance, and their outputs can be combined in a single time series. Over one 73 ha cattle farm in northern Colombia, we tested whether the two platforms yield the same parcel-scale vegetation and water indices and, where they differ, at which layer the difference originates: the product, the processing chain or the scene universe. For identical products, scene classification and harmonised reflectance matched in every comparable pixel, and the same chain executed locally or server-side in GEE gave per-scene indices and monthly medians that agreed within 1e-6. The catalogues, however, did not hold the same scenes: between June 2024 and April 2025, 10 of 146 scene–tile records existed only in GEE, six of them Sentinel-2C records, and none only in MPC; in 22 of 136 common records, all from June–July 2024, the catalogues held different L2A generations of the same acquisition. In the two monthly composites tested over the farm, the GEE-only scenes shifted mean NDVI by −0.0005 and −0.0087; over a public 1 km² demonstration area with the same scene inventory, the shift reached −0.028 (January 2025). Files: - Pantevez-Villamil_2026_GEE-MPC-Sentinel2_preprint_v1.pdf — preprint (English), not peer reviewed. - Pantevez-Villamil_2026_GEE-MPC-Sentinel2_data_v1.zip — reconciliation table with scene identifiers, processing baselines and cloud cover; E2 analysis; scene lists and SHA-256 hashes of each composite; monthly metrics and per-pixel difference distributions; evidence tables for Section 3.2; public demonstration area of interest and tool outputs on it. The farm geometry is not included (landowner privacy). - Pantevez-Villamil_2026_GEE-MPC-Sentinel2_code_v1.0.0.zip — three Python tools (MIT licence), Spanish-language guide, acceptance test and workflow figures. Code in the software archive is released under the MIT licence. Catalogues queried on 24 September 2026. Developed within the Curso de Percepción Remota Avanzada, Doctorado en Agroecología, Facultad de Ciencias Agrarias, Universidad Nacional de Colombia, Sede Bogotá. Generative AI assistants (Claude, Anthropic; ChatGPT, OpenAI) supported test design, code, literature search, review and drafting; the author verified all results and is responsible for the content.
title: Same computation, different scenes: a single-site comparison of Sentinel-2 L2A composites from Google Earth Engine and Microsoft Planetary Computer

summary: This repository contains the curated research inputs, analysis code, and reference outputs supporting the study “Supplier identity can reverse estimates of global irrigation savings.” The study examines whether estimates of global irrigation savings depend on which suppliers reduce production, even when displacement quantities are held fixed within each market. It combines crop production, trade, and water-use data with constrained allocation models, historical production-contraction benchmarks, alternative water accounts, and conditional future scenarios for 2050 and 2100. Repository contents 01_Research_Inputs.xlsx — Curated source observations, geographic and crop identifiers, variable definitions, and source citations. 02_Research_Data.sqlite — Larger input datasets, archived analytical outputs, numerical checks, optional derived checkpoints, and an index linking the release to the associated manuscript and supplementary material. Source inputs and computed outputs are explicitly distinguished. 03_Analysis.py — Consolidated Python code containing the analytical modules, dependency specifications, input verification, and reproduction workflow. 04_Readme.txt — Documentation of data provenance, units, assumptions, reproduction instructions, licensing, and file checksums. The release corresponds to six main-text figures, 16 supplementary figures, and 24 supplementary tables. The exact associated manuscript and supplementary document versions are identified by their SHA-256 fingerprints. Data sources include ACEA, FAOSTAT, CWASI, GCAM scenario outputs, USGS irrigation water-use estimates, Kansas irrigation-technology replication data, and complementary water-account datasets. Source-specific citations and attribution requirements are retained in the documentation. Reproduction and validation The documented workflow uses Python 3.11. Separate dependency environments are specified where required. Installing dependencies requires internet access; the numerical analyses use the deposited inputs. Instructions cover the complete workflow and targeted reproduction checks. For version 1.0.1, file checksums, database integrity, and embedded assets were verified. The full-routing analysis was rerun from the deposited GCAM inputs for all 50 future configurations, reproducing the archived global water bounds and joint conservation outcomes within numerical tolerance. summary: Code, 2.5-D finite-wavelength forward solver, datasets, trained models and result files reproducing every number in the manuscript "Source-Conditioned Neural Surrogates for Magnetotelluric Response Prediction Under Finite-Wavelength Excitation" (S. Oh). The study makes the magnetotelluric source an explicit input of a neural forward surrogate. A validated 2.5-D scattered-field solver for a source of finite along-strike wavelength generates the training data; a conditional U-Net predicts the electromagnetic fields, from which impedance and tipper are reconstructed; an aliasing ratio quantifies how much of a source perturbation a plane-wave inversion re-images as conductivity; a surrogate-domain recoverability experiment returns a source estimate close to the known synthetic value, while a direct solver re-forward shows that the recovered conductivity and wavenumber are not together a solver-consistent inverse solution; and magnetometer arrays at three geomagnetic latitudes place real settings on the dimensionless axis that the model defines. CONTENTS: README.md, LICENSE, DATA_LICENSE.txt and requirements.txt are attached unpacked. The code archive holds the analysis scripts (top level and mt3d/) and the full solver source (solver/, with the dataset generator, the Jacobian dump, the re-forward program and the unit tests); it is MIT licensed except the third-party Triangle library, which is redistributed verbatim under its own terms. The data archive holds the three datasets (dataset_dense, dataset_freq, dataset40), the trained checkpoints (ckpt/, mt3d/ckpt/), the joint-inversion and layered-earth training data (mt3d/*.npz), the plane-wave Jacobian dump (phase3/), the solver sweeps (phase1_repro/) and the result files next to the scripts that write them, all under CC BY 4.0 (DATA_LICENSE.txt). Figures and figure-drawing scripts are not included; every figure is a direct plot of a listed result file. Comments have been removed from all code written for this study. Not included: the magnetometer-array time series, which are third-party open data (EarthScope/USArray MT through the IRIS/EarthScope Data Management Center; AusLAMP Musgraves/APY through AuScope and Geoscience Australia, CC BY 4.0) and are rebuilt from those sources by the archived fetch and conversion scripts; and the field-station file that supplies the period list of the two control tests of Section S-XVII (available from the author on request).
title: Source-Conditioned Residual Learning for Magnetotelluric Responses Under Finite-Wavelength Excitation

summary: EnCert is a compiler-level formal verification framework for checking Namespace-protected LLVM IR produced by the Zeno capability architecture. It decomposes post-transformation verification into two complementary stages: thoroughness verification, which checks that covered memory accesses use valid protected pointers with consistent Namespace size, lifetime, and replacement behavior, and functional-preservation verification, which uses normalization contracts and Alive2 to determine whether the protected program refines the original program for supported valid executions. The artifact includes the EnCert LLVM passes, evaluation scripts, benchmark inputs, controlled mutation infrastructure, and reference results used to reproduce the experiments on EnForge-protected MSET programs, including the detection of protection violations and functional corruptions reported in the paper.
title: EnCert

summary: This repository provides the processed data, analysis code, model outputs, and figure source data supporting the study "Competitive Research Funding and Publication Productivity across Japanese National Universities: A Between- and Within-University Analysis of KAKENHI."   The study examines the association between university-level KAKENHI award activity and publication productivity across Japanese national universities, distinguishing persistent between-university differences from year-to-year within-university variation.   The main analytical dataset covers 85 Japanese national universities from 2021 to 2025. summary: This data and code release accompanies “Output rules and corpus preparation shape retrieval evaluation in a cross-language legal information audit”. Version 3.0 brings together the current rule experiment, internal task benchmark, legal-version evidence and selected research exports from the published version 2.1 baseline. The collection contains 39 Peruvian legal-information records. The output-rule component applies eight combinations of no-match handling, document-support filtering and tie ordering to frozen scores for 32 retained queries and 58 designated-target exposures per language path. It includes 6,912 query-level results, 216 aggregate summaries and a 5,000-replicate shared-order negative control. The internal benchmark contains twelve tasks in six clusters, two formulations per task, 468 provisional content grades, the two returned coding sets, four retrieval configurations and corpus-repair comparisons. Current sensitivity files evaluate existing grade sets, all 27 assignments to three unknown returned grades and RETA-family aggregation. Preparation and judgment roles, prior-output exposure and missing values are retained. Content support is evaluated separately from temporal applicability. The legal-evidence component supplies dated official-source locators, checksums and version findings. summary: The critical exponent ν of Newton’s coupling is the main quantity compared between the functional renormalization group and lattice gravity. In a gauge-independent Einstein–Hilbert approximation it is known in closed form, and optimized regulators were reported to give ν ≈ 1/3, the value found in Regge-calculus simulations. Writing threshold functions as moments over the ratio u = p2/(p2 + Rk) of the regularized to the free propagator, we show that in this approximation 1/ν = (d − 2)(1 + ⟨u⟩), with ⟨u⟩ a weighted mean of u. In four dimensions, exchanging momentum and regulator maps 1/ν to 6 − 1/ν, so every shape function that is its own inverse, including Litim’s and the power-law regulator, gives ν = 1/3 exactly. Litim’s gap criterion is invariant under the exchange and leaves ν free: optimized regulators with finite threshold functions realize all 1/4 < ν < 1/2. The same mechanism acts in the minimal essential scheme: the condition on the inessential vacuum energy involves a threshold function dominated by the ultraviolet tail of the regulator. At second order in derivatives, standard optimized regulators give 1/ν between 2.31 and 2.49, and optimized regulators with longer ultraviolet tails reach the lattice value 1/ν ≈ 3.0. Choosing graviton and ghost regulators so that the vacuum term vanishes removes this dependence and leaves 1/ν between 2.19 and 2.73 for all shapes considered, below the lattice value.
title: The gravitational critical exponent and the shape of the regulator

summary: This record provides the public, non-confidential analytical and reproducibility materials supporting the manuscript “When Does Seismic–Geotechnical Data Fusion Add Value? A Borehole-Aware Empirical-to-Synthetic Validation Framework for Urban Tunnelling.” The study develops and audits a borehole-aware empirical-to-synthetic framework for evaluating whether adding downhole seismic information provides defensible incremental value in predicting the Ménard pressuremeter modulus under held-out validation. The empirical benchmark comprises 41 support-matched pressuremeter–seismic records across 21 independent boreholes from the Isfahan Metro Line 2 investigation. The framework compares a reference model, a geotechnical/geological-depth baseline, a seismic-only branch, naive multimodal fusion, and a dependence-aware fusion branch using leave-one-borehole-out validation. The public release contains a de-identified 41-record benchmark dataset, final manuscript Figure 1–5 assets, the current Supplementary Material and Supplementary Figure S1, released derived analytical outputs, provenance and reproducibility documentation, reproducibility and repository-audit scripts, computational-environment specifications, and SHA-256 integrity information. The de-identified dataset replaces source borehole identifiers with pseudonymous identifiers and excludes borehole coordinates and other spatially identifying source information. The underlying Isfahan Metro Line 2 geotechnical, geophysical, and pressuremeter source records are controlled by the Isfahan Urban Railway Organization and are not publicly redistributable. Original source workbooks, proprietary project documents, spatially identifying information, and other restricted source-derived materials are intentionally excluded from this public archive. Permission was obtained to use and publish the de-identified, non-confidential data extracted from the project report and the derived analytical information included in this release. The public code component provides scripts for reproducing the released manuscript-level benchmark metrics and verifying the integrity and consistency of the deposited files. These scripts do not contain the restricted original project records or proprietary source-data processing materials. The archive is intended to support transparent audit and reproducibility of the released derived analyses while preserving the access restrictions applying to the underlying project data.
title: When Does Seismic–Geotechnical Data Fusion Add Value? — Project 06 Data and Reproducibility Package

summary: Physics-based human-object interaction has achieved robust single-agent manipulation skills, yet extending them to multi-agent cooperative tasks remains challenging. Existing approaches typically adapt interaction policies through task-specific fine-tuning, which entangles low-level contact-rich execution with high-level coordination and limits reuse across object geometries, interaction types, and team sizes. We propose a hierarchical framework that converts a single-agent HOI policy into a reusable Object-oriented Motion Skill. Specifically, we reinterpret teacher rollouts as object-oriented action supervision by extracting short-horizon object-proxy motions from executed trajectories, and distill task-specific teachers into a low-level skill operating in an Object-oriented Action Space. For downstream tasks, the distilled skill is frozen as a reusable executor, while a high-level policy coordinates multiple agents by generating region-wise object-oriented actions conditioned on the shared object, task goal, agent states, and local manipulation regions. This formulation shifts multi-agent HOI learning from direct contact-rich full-body control to compact object-level proxy-motion coordination. Experiments on diverse HOI tasks show that the distilled Object-oriented Motion Skill supports robust proxy-motion execution and enables composable policy learning across different interaction types, object geometries, and team sizes.
title: From Solo to Ensemble: A Hierarchical Framework for Composable Multi-Agent Human-Object Interaction

summary: LLM-based multi-agent systems (MASs) are increasingly used to solve complex tasks through coordinated reasoning, tool use, and interaction with external resources. However, attributing failures in such systems remains challenging because the observed outcome often does not directly reveal the error responsible for the failed execution. In this work, the attribution target is the decisive error, defined as the agent--step pair whose correction would recover the failed execution. Existing approaches largely identify suspicious steps without explicitly modeling how errors propagate across interactions or persist in unresolved loops, making decisive errors difficult to distinguish from downstream failure symptoms. We propose \textbf{E}rror-Propagation \textbf{M}odeling for \textbf{F}ailure \textbf{A}ttribution (\textbf{EMFA}). EMFA constructs a structured representation of the failed trajectory, models both cascading propagation and persistent interaction loops, and uses propagation-aware candidate screening followed by counterfactual verification to identify the decisive agent--step pair. On the Who\&When benchmark, EMFA achieves state-of-the-art step-level attribution accuracy and remains competitive at the agent level. It improves the previous best step-level results by 3.45 and 4.40 percentage points on the Hand-Crafted and Algorithm-Generated subsets, respectively.
title: Error-Propagation Modeling for Failure Attribution in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems

summary: The emerging low-altitude economy demands unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV)-enabled integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) for reliable connectivity and environmental awareness. In particular, embodied UAV agents offer a promising means of supporting autonomous operations through a closed loop linking perception, decision-making, and physical actions. However, each UAV has access only to local observations, and effective cooperation requires exchanging local states and intentions. Directly sharing such information can incur substantial signaling overhead and hinder timely coordination in dynamic environments. To deal with this problem, this paper investigates a cooperative ISAC network of embodied UAV agents and formulates a joint token communications (TokCom) and physical control problem to minimize total propulsion energy subject to communication and sensing rate requirements. Then, we propose a state--intent TokCom (SI-TokCom) framework driven by multi-agent embodied policy learning. Specifically, separate pretrained codebooks enable compact exchanges of local states and intentions, while UAV agents jointly learn to select and compose tokens and determine physical actions based on local observations and received tokens. Simulation results show that SI-TokCom achieves 98.9\% and 99.1\% of the centralized baseline's communication and sensing rates, respectively. Compared with the local baseline, it improves the corresponding rates by 5.0\% and 43.6\%, respectively, with essentially unchanged propulsion energy. These results highlight the potential of TokCom for communication-efficient cooperation among embodied UAV agents in ISAC systems.
title: An Embodied Multiagent Framework Based on Token Communications for Cooperative ISAC

summary: Physics-based models connect scientific explanation with quantitative prediction. Constructing them requires selecting physical processes, defining states and governing equations, specifying couplings, and identifying parameters from experiments. Existing AI systems remain limited in making these model structure decisions autonomously. We introduce EvoSim, a self-evolving AI scientist for physical modeling. It uses experimental discrepancies to drive mechanism and equation revisions and held-out experimental data to test physical plausibility. Exploration traces make updates to knowledge, skills, and multi-agent orchestration. This co-evolution improves physics-based models and EvoSim's ability to select mechanisms, diagnose failures, and coordinate research. We evaluate EvoSim on two industrial battery modeling tasks. It predicts lithium-metal-plating onset from 25 to 45 degrees Celsius and 2 C to 6 C with a mean absolute error of 1.79% in state of charge. Dynamic voltage prediction under vehicle driving conditions achieves a root mean square error of 7.62 mV, surpassing the reported accuracy of models developed by human experts. Self-evolution reduces model and physics errors by approximately 36% relative to baseline, demonstrating improved scientific modeling capability. EvoSim turns experimental observations into validated models and cumulative research expertise.
title: EvoSim: Learning to Model, Modeling to Learn

summary: Offline MARL increasingly relies on generative policies to model multimodal joint behavior, typically by distilling a centralized teacher into decentralized one-step actors under the CTDE. We identify a failure mode at the teacher training stage: standard flow-based teachers pair noise with replay targets independently, so nearby noise samples can be routed toward conflicting coordination modes. The teacher then produces samples between valid modes, and because the distillation loss regresses each local actor onto the conditional mean of the teacher's output given local input, this error is not absorbed but propagated to the student. To remove this teacher-side artifact, we propose Mode-Support Semi-Discrete Optimal Transport (MoSDOT), which summarizes multimodal replay into a finite mode support with prescribed capacities and uses conditional semi-discrete optimal transport to assign each noise sample to a single mode before teacher training. We additionally study a shared-randomness variant that uses a shared noise component at execution to expose the residual gap intrinsic to strict-product execution. On controlled diagnostics and offline MARL benchmarks, MoSDOT improves endpoint quality and routing consistency, particularly on datasets exhibiting multimodal joint behavior.
title: Multi-Agent Coordination via Support-Preserving Distillation

summary: Frontier multimodal foundation models (e.g., GPT-6 Astra) have recently shown strong potential for direct robotic control, yet their performance on fine manipulation remains limited. We argue that an important source of failure is not necessarily insufficient policy capability, but insufficient spatial observability, where task-critical spatial relationships may be poorly revealed by the existing physical camera setup. We introduce SpatialHarness, a test-time embodied harness that provides test-time spatial scaffolding for fine robotic manipulation without policy fine-tuning or changes to the physical sensing setup. SpatialHarness maintains an online simulated scene synchronized with real-world execution, identifies task-critical spatial relationships, and renders complementary virtual views that expose them to a frozen multimodal policy. To keep the simulated scene aligned during interaction, we develop interaction-aware scene synchronization that distinguishes static, held, and transition modes. We evaluate SpatialHarness on four real-robot manipulation tasks spanning precise geometric alignment, object-relative placement, and articulated-object interaction. Using the same frozen GPT-6 Astra policy, SpatialHarness substantially improves task success, including from 26.7% to 66.7% on plug insertion and from 0% to 100% on Tower of Hanoi. These results indicate that improving spatial observability at test time can unlock fine-manipulation capabilities already present in strong multimodal foundation models. Project website: https://emilia113.github.io/SpatialHarness/.
title: SpatialHarness: Test-Time Spatial Scaffolding for Fine Robotic Manipulation

summary: Learning and problem solving depend critically on the structure of internal representations. While many modern data-driven artificial systems achieve strong predictive performance, their learned representations often lack explicit structure for expressing abstraction, invariance, and task-relevant regularities. We propose a minimal structural framework in which representational operations relevant to problem solving, such as context formation, invariance recognition, representative selection, abstraction, and procedural reuse, are made explicit. The central notion is that of a \emph{context}, formalized as a partition of a subset of an underlying state space, which fixes the distinctions, granularity, and form in which a problem can be posed. Within this setting, invariance recognition and representative selection are treated as fundamental representational operations. The framework is realized as a Knowledge Space composed of two coupled graph structures: a Concept Graph that hosts constructed and refined concepts, and a Procedure Graph that encodes typed operations over representations. Together, these structures provide a minimal cognitive-representational algebra for operating on representations without assuming sophisticated inference, learning, control, perception, or motor mechanisms. Using simple illustrative examples and a finite weak-solver demonstration, we show that appropriate representational organization can simplify the form and scope of admissible regularities, even when problem solving is carried out by a fixed and limited solver. The contribution of the paper is structural rather than algorithmic: it identifies representational prerequisites for abstraction, invariance, and procedural reuse in problem solving, and states explicit success and failure conditions for the weak-solver setting.
title: A Structural Theory of Cognitive Representation and Problem Solving,Contexts, Invariance, and the Knowledge Space

summary: Data video is a media form that integrates data visualization with video narrative, widely adopted in news reporting and business analysis. Compared with general video understanding, data video understanding places greater emphasis on accurately reading data from animated charts, integrating evidence across charts and time, and understanding how narrative organization and visual design communicate information. Yet existing benchmarks target either general videos or static charts, and data video understanding has not been systematically evaluated. We present DataVista, the first benchmark for data video understanding, containing 961 real-world data videos and 6,775 evaluation questions organized under a three-level progressive capability framework (data perception, temporal reasoning, narrative understanding) with 10 fine-grained question types across five topic domains. Systematic evaluation of 19 mainstream MLLMs shows that the best-performing model, Gemini-3.1-Pro, achieves 70.0% overall accuracy, still far below human expert performance, with models performing worst on Causal Reasoning and Narrative Structure. Increasing frame counts and adding subtitles mainly benefit data perception and temporal reasoning, with limited gains in narrative understanding. Further analysis of model responses identifies typical failure modes in chart reading, evidence judgment, and instruction understanding. The benchmark is available at https://github.com/HKUSTDial/DataVista.
title: DataVista: Diagnosing Multimodal LLMs on Data Video Understanding

summary: Autoregressive video diffusion enables causal video streaming without a bidirectional pass over the full clip, but existing few-step systems usually retain only the opening and most recent frames in a fixed-size KV cache. Once an event leaves this window, later frames can no longer attend to it, a failure we term mid-horizon forgetting. We present Memory Forcing, a few-step streaming method that preserves this missing history without increasing the cache size. Its Archive \& Working Banks partition the cache into sink, archive, and working regions, retaining diverse intermediate events alongside recent motion under fixed memory. Because absolute temporal indices drift outside the training range, Bank-aware RoPE reassigns indices at attention time so each bank remains distinguishable. At 1.3B, Memory Forcing leads on longer clips, shows the smallest drop from 5s to 60s among methods reporting all four lengths, and preserves subjects and scenes through leave-and-return. The same design scales to Wan2.2 5B, producing more physically plausible, realistic, and dynamic videos and, to our knowledge, the first public 5B model on this forcing line.
title: Memory Forcing: Attendable Mid-Horizon History for Streaming Video Generation

summary: Future 6G networks aim to expose sensing as a native service by reusing communication infrastructure. We study respiration sensing on a cell-free massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) base station, where a 64-antenna channel must be fused into a breathing waveform. The state-of-the-art hand-crafted fusion is near-optimal in benign conditions. It collapses, however, under strong in-band motion interference, whose frequency falls inside the respiration band. We show that a learned complex-weight beamformer recovers respiration by spatial nulling, and that the remaining gap to a per-recording oracle can be closed at deployment by label-free test-time adaptation. Crucially, we identify which label-free signal makes this work. Frequency- and variance-based criteria cannot separate an in-band interferer from breathing. Our spatial-redundancy test-time adaptation (SR-TTA), which maximizes consistency across random antenna subsets under an out-of-band spectral veto, preserves benign performance in our tests. The respiration-rate error drops from 5.8 to 0.8 breaths per minute (bpm) under simulated in-band interference, and the pipeline maps onto the Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN) architecture as O-RAN distributed-unit (O-DU) range-gating, an adaptation xApp, and a calibration rApp. On real testbed recordings, a one-time cross-subject calibration plus SR-TTA reduces failures from 47% to 7%, drawing level with the hand-crafted combiner using label-free test-time adaptation.
title: SR-TTA: Spatial-Redundancy Test-Time Adaptation for Interference-Robust Respiration Sensing

summary: Some defects in an AI-generated study can be identified from its artifacts; others require knowledge of what was approved before execution. We propose study contracts that bind declared experimental choices, run obligations and claim scope to recorded execution evidence, and distinguish this contract-relative verification from scientific truth. A diagnostic using eight self-authored clean/mutated pairs illustrates the information boundary. A deterministic checker applying a registered, fault-specific rule to approved and executed objects detected all eight registered mutations. Across eighteen recorded judge aliases given individual metadata-filtered packages without pair context or the registry-selected fault label, 104 of 144 mutated evaluation cases received defect flags; the remaining cases comprised 32 abstentions and eight terminal failures, with no explicit clean decisions on mutated cases. Some packages retained approval and execution fields, including digests. The prompt instructed judges to abstain when evidence was insufficient. These results characterize a deliberately information-asymmetric development setting; they do not isolate the effect of authoritative information from differences in task specification and rule selection, and they are not comparative verifier quality or agent reward hacking. We identify full-information comparisons, legitimate-adaptation controls and closed-loop agent evaluations as necessary tests of whether contract checks improve useful compliant completion under optimization.
title: What Output-Only Review Cannot Verify: Study Contracts for Research Agents

summary: LLM agents can spend millions of tokens during vulnerability discovery without producing a working proof of concept (PoC). What consumes that budget, and why does it fail to produce results? We diagnose these costs and failures through a multi-axis open-coding study of 200 CyberGym traces, spanning four agents (i.e., Codex, OpenCode, Cybench, and EnIGMA) under an unaided baseline and four existing efficiency methods. The study reveals three key findings. First, different agents vary substantially in success and cost, and higher spending does not consistently yield better outcomes. Second, code localization and understanding, together with vulnerability reasoning and trigger design, account for 60.4% of tokens and represent the two leading bottlenecks in failed runs. Third, only 24.4% of matched comparisons preserve success at lower total cost; unsuitable signals and auxiliary overhead limit the benefits of existing methods. Motivated by these findings, we present AVRI, an Agent-centric Vulnerability Reasoning Interface built around a persistent Bidirectional Evidence Trace (BET). BET connects how the harness consumes input with the conditions required to make a selected operation unsafe, retaining source-supported correspondences alongside the agent's hypotheses and open questions. Reading, analysis, and persistence commands help agents build and reuse this evidence rather than repeatedly retrieve and reconstruct it. On 20 evaluation tasks, AVRI reduces total cost by 18.0% for Codex and 23.7% for OpenCode while preserving success rates and improving or maintaining recall.
title: Where Do the Tokens Go? Understanding and Reducing Costs in LLM Agents for Vulnerability Discovery

BET connects how the harness consumes input with the conditions required to make a selected operation unsafe, retaining source-supported correspondences alongside the agent's hypotheses and open questions. Reading, analysis, and persistence commands help agents build and reuse this evidence rather than repeatedly retrieve and reconstruct it. On 20 evaluation tasks, AVRI reduces total cost by 18.0% for Codex and 23.7% for OpenCode while preserving success rates and improving or maintaining recall.
title: Where Do the Tokens Go? Understanding and Reducing Costs in LLM Agents for Vulnerability Discovery

summary: We establish the overarching mathematical physics framework underlying gravitational screening and electroweak mixing in Big Boot Gauge Theory (BBGT). To demonstrate that the transition from the bare gravitational constant G_bare = 6.514085763e-11 m^3 kg^-1 s^-2 (derived from CODATA 2022 constants under unit space-time momentum p = mc = 1 kg m s^-1) to the observed value G_obs = 6.67430e-11 m^3 kg^-1 s^-2 is a rigorous topological necessity rather than an arbitrary post-hoc adjustment, we formulate the screening dynamics using Möbius inversion on finite posets over the subgroup lattice of Poincaré Dodecahedral Space (S^3/I^*). We prove that non-associative transit across the e_4 Pati-Salam midpoint node acts as a Möbius topological twist, fixing the geometric inverse-square screening factor S_ZIP^-2 = (1 - 1/120)^-2 = 1.016877348. Combining this with longitudinal Z-leakage (delta_Z = 0.026892000) and non-associative midpoint transit corrections (Delta_assoc = 0.000092701) yields the exact screened laboratory constant without arbitrary tuning.  Furthermore, we demonstrate that the weak mixing angle (sin^2 theta_W = 1/5 + 1/32 = 0.23125) originates from the pentagonal P_5 symmetry order of the dodecahedron combined with a 2^5 chiral energy cascade, agreeing with experiment (0.23122) to within 0.01%. Finally, we present the complete 8x8 Logical Transitive Index Matrix (T_{n->m}), showing how the 10^19 Planck-to-electroweak mass hierarchy is compressed down to a discrete compilation factor of 128.35 across the aethereal boot levels.
