summary: Multi-agent path finding (MAPF) solvers are evaluated on the schedules they produce, not on how well those schedules can be executed. Specifically, continuous-time optimal solvers can achieve even lower cost than their discrete counterparts by scheduling agents with near-zero temporal/spatial separation, and by exploiting graphs with higher connectedness; however, such schedules may prove hard to execute under a realistic controller. We integrate AOC-CBS, an anytime-optimal continuous-time MAPF solver, into a fleet coordination framework in which each agent tracks its timed path using model predictive control, and we evaluate the resulting system on congested MovingAI benchmark instances with 21 to 40 agents. Without intervention, only a fraction of the instances complete execution. We then apply T-robustness by adding a time-margin, i.e., a minimum temporal gap between agents at shared locations, as well as spatial inflation of the agent footprint. Increasing either margin raises execution success, for a relatively small increase in the schedule's sum-of-costs; it also improves how closely agents adhere to the schedule: when tracking each agent's position throughout execution and comparing it against the position it should occupy according to the schedule, the mean discrepancy falls significantly as the margin increases. In general, the two margins have different effects; temporal margin decreases deviation, giving the controller room to stay on schedule. Spatial margin affects deviation less and instead increases the clearance between agents, so that the same deviation no longer leads to a blocking stall. They are nonetheless substitutes rather than complements: spatial inflation is almost free in schedule cost, but its effect on execution success is small and does not compound with a temporal margin already in place.
title: The Cost of Executability: Temporal Margins for Continuous-Time Multi-Agent Path Finding under Closed-Loop Control

summary: Digital advertising is an important means for platforms to reach potential users and drive business growth. Advertising delivery is the core link between marketing objectives and actual returns. Existing methods have achieved partial automation in individual tasks such as bidding and budget allocation, but they still rely on human operators for overall coordination, making it difficult to support large-scale operations. They also often fail to achieve optimal performance, and individual experience remains difficult to turn into reusable operational capabilities. In addition, as advertising markets change, advertising delivery systems need timely strategy updates to remain effective in dynamic markets. To automate the entire advertising operations process and improve adaptability to market changes, we propose AdCoEvo, a co-evolving multi-agent advertising delivery system. Specifically, the system connects delivery decisions across different timescales and operational granularities through role specialization. Diagnostic results guide account planning and strategy adjustment in the next period. The multi-agent system updates its model parameters based on actual delivery outcomes and continually improves delivery strategies through mutual feedback among planning, adjustment, and diagnosis, thereby achieving co-evolution. Experiments show that, relative to the rule-based operational baseline (Rule), AdCoEvo increases advertiser value by 14.02% while reducing cost per acquisition by 7.07%. Compared with a multi-agent system with fixed parameters, AdCoEvo increases advertiser value by 3.96% and reduces cost per acquisition by 1.24%, indicating that co-evolution can yield greater delivery returns.
title: AdCoEvo: A Co-Evolving Multi-Agent Advertising Delivery System

summary: We provide a distributed online algorithm for multi-agent submodular coordination in bandit environments, i.e., environments whose evolution is unknown a priori and may even adapt to the agents' actions. We are motivated by multi-robot tasks such as target tracking, where the optimal actions change over time and the agents must track them rather than a single fixed optimum. To address such problems, we provide the Optimistic Distributed Online Greedy (O-DOG) algorithm, that leverages predictions about the environment's behavior and improves regret guarantees. The agents select actions simultaneously over arbitrary, possibly time-varying, network topologies, and each agent acts optimistically, i.e., leveraging predictions of its upcoming rewards, e.g., from forecasts of the targets' motion and of its neighbors' actions. We bound O-DOG's tracking regret in terms of the agents' prediction error and the bound never exceeds its prediction-free counterpart. Particularly, it is sublinear even when the optimal action changes at every time step, provided the predictions are accurate enough. We further quantify the suboptimality due to decentralization as a function of the network structure, and show that accurate predictions accelerate convergence. We validate O-DOG in simulated multi-robot target tracking.
title: Optimistic Distributed Submodular Coordination with Applications to Multi-Target Tracking with Multiple Robots

summary: AUTONOMOUS NANOROBOTIC NAVIGATION AND MISSION OBSERVABILITY AT THE LIMIT First-Generation Research Flagship 01 | NANO/MICRO ROBOTICS, POWER & MISSION ENDURANCE Feng Cheng-en (33) x Starli This research atlas asks a difficult engineering question: when low-Reynolds-number microfluidic flows, Brownian orientation noise, boundary adhesion, external field actuation and incomplete sensing all influence a micro/nanorobot, what would justify calling its behavior autonomous navigation rather than externally assisted motion? The volume treats navigation as an auditable, bounded mission instead of an attractive trajectory. It develops a five-layer program spanning stochastic hydrodynamics, instrument and actuation provenance, uncertainty-calibrated belief-state estimation, blinded microfluidic challenges and independent requalification. Thirty linked mathematical stations differentiate physical relations, information-theoretic functionals and proposed navigation utility measures, with assumptions, dimensions and possible falsifiers. Eighty-two research chapters each open with a core mathematical relation, followed by five independent single-page research sections. Two hundred detailed Research Gates describe decisive comparisons, confounding explanations, evidence requirements, failure conditions and successor handoff artifacts. Thirty-three provisional Phoenix Answer Embryos offer revisionable research prototypes rather than predetermined conclusions. The key comparator is an equal-budget experiment: fixed-field sequences, microscope-assisted manual control, externally tracked predictive control and candidate fused navigation are evaluated under matched total energy, information access, geometry, time, collision limits and recovery obligations. The manuscript emphasizes blind targets, flow reversal, sensor dropouts, wall adhesion, correlated observations, full-system power accounting, censored failures and post-mission retrieval. A mission arriving at its target but leaving an unrecovered device is not counted as a fully closed success. This work is a hypothesis-generating Research Atlas v1.0, not an experimental report or a validated medical technology. External magnetic, acoustic, optical and microscope infrastructure must be disclosed; no in-vivo or clinical competence is inferred from bench-top movement. Foundational DOI-linked literature provides context, not proof of the proposed integrated system. Every major claim is designed to be revised, rejected or reconstructed by a successor team using raw evidence and pre-registered falsification rules. The current child manuscript does not yet have an independent DOI; one would be assigned only upon actual repository deposit. Editorial release note: the manuscript prioritizes non-duplicative research content and independent testability over an artificial word-count target. It is suitable as a research architecture for additional scientific review, not a substitute for physical validation.

summary: This release provides the data and code supporting a simulation-only study of reference-assisted radiofrequency fracture sensing under anatomical domain shift. It includes 5,580 corrected noise-free RF acquisitions, 356,400 feature rows from 20 independent noise repetitions, model predictions, calibration outputs and paired H2 statistical analyses. MATLAB and Python source code, fixed analysis specifications, figure-generation code and provenance records are included. The materials support reproducible evaluation of independent healthy references and source-locked decision thresholds across five idealised anatomical locations. All data are simulated and do not establish clinical diagnostic accuracy.
title: Data and Code for Machine Learning Based Reference Assisted Signal Recovery Under Anatomical Domain Shift in Simulated Radiofrequency Fracture Sensing

summary: NANOROBOTIC CARGO TRANSPORT AND MICROSCALE MANIPULATION INTEGRITY AT THE LIMIT First-Generation DOI Fission Research Flagship 02 | Starli Active Nanosystems Feng Cheng-en (33) x Starli | Research Atlas v1.0 (October 2026) How can a micro/nanorobotic carrier demonstrate that the object arriving at a designated target is the same intact cargo that was originally loaded, that it was completely and correctly released, and that the carrier or its residues have been accounted for? This English-language research atlas converts cargo-delivery and micromanipulation demonstrations into a falsifiable end-to-end mission-integrity problem. The research develops a five-layer architecture for source identity and material tolerance, microscale contact mechanics, independently observable mission-state transitions, adversarial fault injection, and blind cross-platform requalification. Thirty mathematically distinct derivation stations connect probabilistic joint-task qualification to chemical mass balance, optical-label dissociation, surface adsorption, force-dependent detachment, microcontact mechanics, drag, kinetic release, spatial uncertainty, carryover contamination, whole-facility energy accounting, missing-fate bounds and hard safety vetoes. Eighty-two chapters each have a dedicated core-equation opening and five separate research sections. Two hundred Research Gates propose independent comparisons, physical perturbations, competing explanations, measurable failure criteria and reproducibility artifacts. Thirty-three provisional Phoenix Answer Embryos outline candidate systems that future investigators are invited to overturn, repair or rebuild. A machine-readable research atlas and formula-gate-DOI index enable AI-assisted comparison and future research reuse. The central endpoint is a correlated joint event: correct cargo identity and integrity, correct target, independently confirmed release, and verified carrier retrieval or authorized terminal disposition. The manuscript insists on counting every initiated mission rather than multiplying attractive substep success rates. It also distinguishes visible fluorescence from chemically intact cargo, externally actuated manipulation from on-board autonomy, and destination arrival from complete task closure. Strong benchmarks include optical tweezers, established magnetic-bead handling, microfluidic conveyance and conventional microgrippers under matched task difficulty, time and whole-facility energy use. Research status: This is a hypothesis-generating, nonclinical experimental-design atlas; it reports no newly conducted cargo experiments, clinical performance or proven integrated device. Foundational and recent DOI-identified publications provide engineering context but do not validate its new claims. The 200 Gates are open problems, not accomplished results. The actual text length and layout follow the substance of individual chapters rather than an artificially enforced 100,000-word count. Individual child DOI: not minted in this manuscript-production workflow.

summary: This replication package contains the experimental artifacts, anonymized empirical benchmark dataset (N = 5,000 paired student-opportunity records), statistical verification scripts, database definitions, and microservices source code for the research paper: "Hybrid Vector-Temporal Matching for Student Freelance Placement: An Empirical Study of Database-Level Vector Offloading" Targeted for Information and Software Technology (IST, Elsevier). Package Contents: data/: Anonymized benchmark dataset (students_data_tesis_final.csv) featuring 168-hour weekly availability matrices and raw ablation output. benchmarks/: Automated Python scripts for Stratified 5-fold cross-validation ablation (C1 to C4), Wilcoxon Signed-Rank hypothesis testing, Cliff's Delta effect size calculation, and bootstrap confidence intervals. database/: PostgreSQL 16 schema and stored procedure definitions for HNSW Approximate Nearest Neighbor vector search (pgvector) and dynamic schedule intersection. turborepo-src/: Clean source code of the decoupled microservices monorepo (API Gateway, Matching Service, ML Engine, and shared Protocol Buffers). System Requirements: Python 3.10+ with NumPy, SciPy, Pandas, Scikit-Learn, and NLTK. Node.js v20+ / pnpm v9+ and Docker Engine for microservice orchestration.
title: Replication Package: Hybrid Vector-Temporal Matching for Student Freelance Placement

summary: We have presented a mathematically closed, comprehensive foundation for the C861 discrete spectral benchmark. By establishing the exact rank-two projector geometry, resolving Dirichlet sum cancellations, providing constructive proofs for linear B-spline KAN operator reproduction, and formalizing the Lyapunov convergence of Dense Associative Memory on spherical manifolds, this framework eliminates ambiguities in evaluating learned physical operators. Furthermore, the spectral interlacing analysis of the CN → PN structural homotopy equips the scientific machine learning community with a tool to distinguish authentic topological sensitivity from numerical discretization artifacts.
title: Exact Discrete Spectral Invariants as a Falsification Baseline for Learned Operator

summary: Code, BOLD record identifiers and result tables behind the article "Calibrated uncertainty for reference-free species delimitation from DNA barcodes" (H. Ghanem and R. Daou, submitted to Computational Biology and Chemistry). The archive contains the full analysis notebook, scripts that reproduce the ASAP calibration audit and redraw Figures 1–5, the BOLD process ID of every record used (training families Tephritidae, Nymphalidae and Culicidae; cold-test family Carabidae; rare-species and calibration-audit pools), and the result tables behind every number, table and figure in the paper. See README.md for contents and instructions.

summary: Level-2 (restricted) archive, version 1.0.1, of the replication package of the article Auditing successor selection in software repository mining: Evidence from filtering AI-attributed commits (H. Jeong, Hanyang University ERICA; manuscript under review). The public Level-1 archive with the programs, tests and aggregate results is https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23226958 (all versions; version 1.0.3, cited in the manuscript: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23430269). Changes in 1.0.1: two files with the per-identity counts of the exploratory published-measure analysis (file-based churn, cohort B; Supplementary Section S13 of the article) were added, re-keyed like the other cohort-B files; every file of version 1.0.0 is unchanged. The files are per-unit derived counts of the 3,687 cohort-A accounts and the cohort-B identities, with random identifiers (marker dates reduced to the month; no account names, e-mail addresses, repository names, commit SHAs or commit times). Placed by python3 reproduce.py --level2 <folder> of the Level-1 package (version 1.0.3), they recompute the registered aggregates and the exploratory aggregates that do not require the raw commit logs, including rates, transitions, paired contrasts, random-exclusion benchmarks and bootstrap intervals; on Python 3.10.12 with numpy 2.2.6 (Linux, aarch64) and on Python 3.13.16 with numpy 2.5.3 (Linux, x86_64) every regenerated result agreed with the reported one (numerical values within 1e-9, text files identical apart from line endings). Access is restricted because cohort-B rows keep the positions of their repositories in the public sampling order, which the registered repository-cluster bootstrap needs. Access is granted to researchers who state their name, affiliation and purpose and who agree to use the files only to verify, reproduce or extend the analyses of the article, not to redistribute the files or per-unit derivatives, not to attempt any re-identification or linkage to public commit histories or accounts, to store the files securely and delete them when the work is complete, and to cite the article and both archives (ACCESS.md). Reviewers of the article receive an access link through the editor.
title: Replication package (Level 2, restricted) for "Auditing successor selection in software repository mining: Evidence from filtering AI-attributed commits"

summary: Level-1 (public) replication package, version 1.0.3, of the article Auditing successor selection in software repository mining: Evidence from filtering AI-attributed commits (H. Jeong, Hanyang University ERICA; manuscript under review). It accompanies version 3.7 of the manuscript and supersedes version 1.0.2 (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23428669). Changes in 1.0.3: an exploratory analysis applies the fixed-anchor audit to a published file-based churn measure in cohort B ( jss_v2/exploratory_v37/ : the dated plan of 2026-10-17, whose SHA-256 is recorded in both deviation logs, the program w2_file_churn.py and its tests; aggregate results in jss_v2/results/v37/ ). The supplement (version 3.7) adds Section S13 with Tables S58 to S60 and names the exploratory convention for the anchor's own block the anchor-retained convention; the figure programs label that convention accordingly and write 800-dpi RGB TIFF files, with unchanged figure data. reproduce.py runs the new tests, checks the hash of the second dated plan and, with --level2 , recomputes the new aggregate from version 1.0.1 of the Level-2 archive. The registered code and every aggregate result of version 1.0.2 are unchanged, so the SHA-256 values registered in OSF hyf36 and 7jasg still match. Contents: the audit tool (Python, standard library only) with its 47 automated tests and a synthetic example; the registered analysis programs, whose SHA-256 values match those registered in OSF hyf36 (cohort A) and OSF 7jasg (cohort B); the exploratory programs with the dated plans of 2026-10-08 and 2026-10-17 and the record-level conformance checker; aggregate results for every table and figure; the deviation logs of both registrations; the 22-study literature evidence matrix; the cohort-B sampling frame and collection programs; and the generators of the supplement and the figures. Run python3 reproduce.py (Python 3.10 or later, numpy, matplotlib and git). It checks the registered hashes, runs the tests and the synthetic example, and regenerates the supplement tables and the figure data from the aggregate results. With --level2 <folder> it also recomputes, from the restricted per-unit files of the Level-2 archive (version 1.0.1: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23430270), every registered aggregate and every exploratory aggregate that does not require the source commit logs, and compares every regenerated file with the shipped result. Before release, both levels passed on Python 3.10.12 with numpy 2.2.6 (Linux, aarch64) and on Python 3.13.16 with numpy 2.5.3 (Linux, x86_64), there also with every text output written with CRLF line endings. summary: This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview at https://prereview.org/reviews/23432006 . The paper (arXiv 2610.21914) is a pre-registered study of 465 merged agent-authored pull requests from 246 repositories (Sections 3.2-3.5). A frozen pipeline of four review agents and one fix agent ran every PR with three LLMs, and one mixed model per LLM tests CodeHealth against log total tokens (Sections 3.6-3.9). Each CodeHealth point goes with 3.5% to 6.1% lower token cost (Section 4.2, Table 8), but adding the size of the scored files absorbs the coefficient (Section 4.6.4, Table 15). I liked the handling of the pre-registration: the disclosure that review sessions started before filing, the amendment with a full re-collection of the 67 affected PRs (Section 3.12), and the file-size refit that weakens your own headline. I read it as a practitioner who runs coding agents every day. In my company the software development is done by AI agents, so maybe my practical side is useful here. Four comments. 1. On heavy tails (Sections 3.9, 4.2) - you note that one pilot PR was about 45% of a tier's mean token total, while in the main collection no PR exceeded 8.2% of a tier's token sum. In my measurement of 722 agent sessions (150,902 model calls, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22759216), about 3% of sessions gave 80% of the modeled cost. Sessions longer than 200 calls (8% of sessions) gave more than 90% of the money. So in my data the average is driven by a thin tail. What share of each LLM's tokens comes from the top 10% of PRs, and does the CodeHealth slope hold without them? 2. On cache and price (Section 3.8, Table 4, Section 6.3) - the outcome is input plus output tokens, with cached input recorded separately. In the same 722 sessions, more than 85% of the modeled cost was work with context (cache reads and cache writes). In a separate run of 168 sessions, 94.4% of billed tokens were re-reading context already sent (contextburn, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22712985). That is a share of tokens, not of the bill, because cached reads are the cheapest tokens. So a raw token total and a bill can rank PRs differently. Could you refit H1 with cached input priced at each provider's cache-read rate? 3. On paging long files (Sections 3.6, 5.2, 3.13) - the paper links the extra iterations to the 500-line limit per read call. In my guides I write that quality drops as the agent's context fills, and that heavy reading should go to a subagent so the main conversation stays clean. Since tool results are appended to the message history (Section 3.6), paging the median unhealthy-tier file of 2,146 lines puts every page into history that is re-sent on every later call. From the session records, can you count file-read calls and repeat reads of the same file per tier? That would test the paging explanation directly. 4. On the cost of what (Sections 5.5, 5.6, 6.3) - the study does not assess whether comments are correct or fixes are good. In my guides I write that every task needs its own check the agent can run. Without it, "looks done" is the only signal the agent has. I also use a second, fresh agent whose job is to refute the first one, because AI sounds equally sure when it is right and when it is wrong. For the 27-PR replication subsample (Section 3.11), you could run the repository tests after the fix and have a fresh agent try to refute each comment. Tokens per surviving finding would be a cheap first step toward Section 5.6. Thank you for a clear and useful paper. Competing interests Yes: the text cites the author's own technical reports (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22759216, 10.5281/zenodo.22712985); no connection to the article's authors. Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) The author declares that they used generative AI to come up with new ideas for their review.
title: PREreview of "CodeHealth Predicts the Token Cost of Agentic Code Review: A Pre-Registered Study of 465 Agent-Authored Pull Requests"

summary: This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a Structured PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview at https://prereview.org/reviews/23431625 . Does the introduction explain the objective of the research presented in the preprint? Yes The introduction clearly explains the research objectives. It states that the study aims to replicate the quantitative analysis of Krause, Krause, and Bränfors (2018), assess the reproducibility of their findings, and examine potential limitations concerning statistical power and model specification. Are the methods well-suited for this research? Somewhat appropriate The replication approach is suitable for the research, as the authors reproduce the original Cox proportional hazards models and robustness tests. However, the methodological assessment has some gaps. In particular, the power analysis reports values of 0.44 and 0.99 without providing the formula, software procedure, or sufficient calculation details to allow readers to reproduce the estimates. The choice of 42 events in Table 6 also needs clarification, given that Table 5 reports 54 events overall. Additionally, the differences between the original and reproduced sample sizes remain unexplained. These issues weaken the transparency and reproducibility of the analysis. Are the conclusions supported by the data? Somewhat supported The main conclusion is that the original findings can be reproduced, which is supported by the reported results. The authors also reasonably identify the small number of female-signatory agreements and the limitations of drawing causal conclusions from the observed association. However, the claim that the analysis has low statistical power relies on a calculation for which the formula and detailed procedure are not provided (Table 6). The differences between the original and reproduced sample sizes also remain unexplained. These limitations make some aspects of the interpretation less conclusive than they could be. Are the data presentations, including visualizations, well-suited to represent the data? Somewhat appropriate and clear The survival analysis and regression tables are suitable for presenting the findings. However, some numerical inconsistencies in the descriptive statistics and differences in sample sizes across the original and reproduced models need clarification to ensure the results are presented accurately. For instance, Table 3 presents: three major statistical flaws: 1: Conflict Intensity row, where Female Signatories = 1: has SD of 1.2 while the Max is 0.45, which is statistically incorrect. Similarly, (2) Democracy row where Female Signatories = 1, has Mean 0.92 < Min 1. And lastly, on page 5, UN peacekeeping is written as a binary number, however, in Table 3, the binary UN Peacekeeping has Max > 1. All these minor inconsistencies require clarification. How clearly do the authors discuss, explain, and interpret their findings and potential next steps for the research? Very clearly The authors explain their findings, acknowledge the limitations of the small number of agreements with female signatories, and discuss the implications for causal interpretation. They also identify the need for further research, although the power analysis and differences in sample sizes could be explained more transparently. Is the preprint likely to advance academic knowledge? Somewhat likely If the author clarified the sample-size discrepancies and documented the power analysis more transparently, then it would substantially contribute to the reproducibility of an influential finding, as it already highlights the reproducibility of the findings and highlights the limitations in statistical power and causal interpretation. Would it benefit from language editing? No The languages is clear and no major errors could be found hinderig the understanding of the resarch. However some minor issues could be corrected, such as, constant capitalisation of the first letter in column names. Would you

summary: Background: Long-segment intramedullary cervical cord lesions can present a diagnostic challenge, particularly when imaging findings raise suspicion of an intramedullary neoplasm. Differentiating a syrinx from an intramedullary tumor is important for operative planning, as the surgical strategy may differ substantially. Case presentation: A 43-year-old female presented with a six-month history of progressive cervical pain with radicular symptoms, vertigo, left upper-limb sensory disturbance, and impaired left-hand grip. Neurological examination revealed preserved motor power of 5/5 in all four limbs, normal reflexes, and reduced functional grip in the left hand. MRI of the cervical spine demonstrated a long-segment expansile intramedullary lesion extending from the cervicomedullary junction to C7, without contrast enhancement. The radiological report also described Chiari malformation and syringomyelia. Given the diagnostic uncertainty and progressive symptoms, we performed urgent surgical exploration within two days of admission. We performed a C3–C7 laminoplasty to provide multilevel posterior access while preserving the laminar elements without instrumented fixation. Following durotomy and midline myelotomy, a syrinx was identified, with no obvious intramedullary tumor. Syringotomy and drainage were performed, and adjacent spinal cord tissue was obtained for biopsy. Graft duraplasty and reconstruction of the elevated laminae were completed. The patient had an uncomplicated postoperative course, with relief of pain and vertigo and resolution of sensory symptoms. She was discharged with intact motor power and improved but residual left-hand grip weakness. Follow-up MRI demonstrated cord decompression and drainage of the syrinx. Conclusion: This case illustrates the diagnostic uncertainty that may arise when a long-segment non-enhancing intramedullary cervical lesion is suspected to represent a tumor. Intraoperative findings guided the surgical procedure toward syringotomy and drainage, with tissue sampling to investigate a possible underlying neoplasm. Multilevel laminoplasty provided posterior access while allowing reconstruction of the cervical laminar elements. Histopathological confirmation and longer-term follow-up remain necessary.
tags: Cervical syringomyelia; Chiari malformation; intramedullary spinal cord lesion; laminoplasty; syringotomy; duraplasty; diagnostic dilemma.
title: Multilevel Cervical Laminoplasty and Syringotomy for a Long-Segment Cervical Syrinx Mimicking an Intramedullary Tumor: A Case Report

summary: This paper interprets black holes as information relay stations under global unitarity and fast scrambling. It connects holographic encoding, entanglement, Hayden–Preskill recovery, and Page-curve behaviour into a framework describing how infalling information is recorded and redistributed into radiation correlations. The central contribution is the separation of record and relay functions. Recording occurs on the scrambling timescale, while substantial recovery of information deposited before the Page time occurs near the Page transition. Unitary qubit models with up to fourteen black-hole qubits examine these connections using a mutual-information recovery proxy, revealing the role of early radiation and an approximately logistic recovery transition. Two model-specific predictions are proposed: gravitational-wave echoes spaced approximately by the scrambling time, conditional on a reflecting surface at a Planck-scale distance above the horizon; and a recovery transition whose rate remains of order one as system size increases, testable in quantum simulators. The contribution is a functional synthesis supported by model calculations. Keywords: black hole information paradox, holography, unitarity, Hayden–Preskill protocol, Page curve, information relay station, scrambling time, gravitational-wave echoes.
title: Black Holes as Information Relay Stations: A Six-Principle Synthesis from Holography to Unitarity

summary: Експертна методика визначає стадії та операції дослідження, однак сама їх послідовність іще не пояснює, за яких умов результатом однієї операції можна скористатися в наступній. У судовій гірничотехнічній експертизі найбільш відповідальними є переходи від відомостей, що їх містять матеріали, до реконструкції механізму події, від реконструкції – до оцінювання причинного значення обставин, а від установленої дії або бездіяльності – до її технічного співвіднесення з функціями конкретної особи. Мета роботи полягає у формуванні критеріїв, за якими придатність проміжного результату перевіряють до його застосування в наступній операції, та у з’ясуванні зв’язку між фактичною основою – сукупністю достатніх, узгоджених і простежуваних відомостей – і допустимими межами підсумкової відповіді експерта. Дослідження поєднало структурне моделювання, формально-логічний аналіз експертного міркування, зіставлення з положеннями судової експертології та теоретико-методичне узагальнення професійного досвіду у сфері судової гірничотехнічної експертизи. Застосування моделі проілюстровано на двох знеособлених типізованих ситуаціях із завершеної експертної практики 2015–2023 років, що відображають різний стан фактичної основи. Обґрунтовано поняття критерію контрольованого переходу й сім функціональних контрольних точок: відповідності питання компетенції експерта; достатності матеріалів; узгодженості та простежуваності відомостей; можливості реконструкції механізму; причинного значення обставин; суб’єктно-функціонального співвіднесення; синтезу й оцінювання результатів. Для фіксації методичного рішення запропоновано статуси контрольованого переходу: Т+ – дозволений перехід, Т± – обмежено дозволений перехід, Т– – недозволений перехід. Практичними результатами є модель проходження контрольної точки, матриця методичних рішень і структура робочої карти, придатні для використання як методичний модуль судової гірничотехнічної експертизи. Застосування критеріїв контрольованого переходу пов’язує стан фактичної основи з допустимим напрямом подальшого аналізу й запобігає формулюванню відповіді поза обумовленими межами.
title: Критерії контрольованого переходу між операціями судово-експертного дослідження як засіб забезпечення обґрунтованості висновку в судовій гірничотехнічній експертизі

summary: Abstract : Background: The production of high-quality planting material during the nursery stage is essential for establishing productive, competitive, and sustainable oil palm plantations. Genetic material and container type may influence seedling development. Objective: To evaluate the growth of seedlings of two oil palm varieties, Deli × Compacta and Compacta × Ghana (Elaeis guineensis Jacq.), produced using two container types. Methods: The experiment was conducted in Macuspana, Tabasco, Mexico. Seedling growth was evaluated in two varieties, Deli × Compacta and Compacta × Ghana, using tube containers and plastic bags. A randomized complete block design was established with four treatments and four replications, with 100 seedlings per replication (400 seedlings per treatment; 1,600 seedlings in total). Plant height, number of leaves, and stipe diameter were measured every 15 days over 180 days. The same agronomic management was applied to all treatments. Descriptive statistics, analysis of variance (ANOVA), and Tukey’s multiple comparison test. Results: Significant differences among treatments were detected for the evaluated growth variables. For plant height, T3 (Compacta × Ghana in tube containers; CxGt) showed the greatest value at 180 days, reaching 68.37 ± 0.61 cm. For number of leaves, T1 (Deli × Compacta in tube containers; DxCt) and T3 (Compacta × Ghana in tube containers; CxGt) recorded 12.95 ± 0.11 and 12.38 ± 0.10 leaves, respectively, at 180 days. For stipe diameter, T1 and T2 showed the highest values at 180 days, with 2.21 ± 0.03 and 2.19 ± 0.03 cm, respectively, whereas T4 recorded 1.95 ± 0.02 cm. Conclusions: Under the conditions evaluated, seedlings produced in tube containers showed greater plant height and number of leaves at the end of the nursery period. Stipe diameter was higher in the Deli × Compacta material than in the Compacta × Ghana material at 180 days. These results support the potential use of tube containers for nursery production.

title: Growth of Seedlings of two Oil Palm Varieties (Elaeis guineensis Jacq.) in the Nursery Using two Container Types

summary: Background: Hyperlipidemia is a major risk factor for atherosclerosis and cardiovascular diseases. Evaluating drug utilization patterns provides critical insights into clinical practice and rational medicine use. Aim: To analyze the drug utilization patterns, clinical characteristics, and treatment outcomes among patients with hyperlipidemia in a hospital setting. Methodology: A retrospective observational study was conducted involving 150 hyperlipidemic patients receiving lipid-lowering pharmacotherapy at Visva Medical Centre and Hospital. Demographic data, prescribed treatment regimens, baseline, and post-treatment lipid profiles (Total Cholesterol, LDL, HDL, and Triglycerides) were collected and analyzed. Statistical significance was assessed using p-values. Results: Among the 150 participants, males constituted 53.33% (n=80) and females 46.67% (n=70). The majority of patients belonged to the 41–50 age group (n=42) and were classified as overweight based on BMI (n=65). Statin monotherapy was the predominant treatment choice. Atorvastatin was the most frequently prescribed agent (38.00%, n=57), followed by Rosuvastatin (26.67%, n=40), and Fenofibrate (20.00%, n=30). Combination therapy was prescribed in 15.34% (n=23) of patients. Post-treatment evaluation demonstrated statistically significant improvements across all lipid parameters (p < 0.001). Rosuvastatin monotherapy achieved the lowest current mean LDL level (114.35 mg/dL), Atorvastatin showed the highest mean HDL level (50.70 mg/dL), and Fenofibrate + Atorvastatin combination achieved the lowest triglyceride levels (161.60 mg/dL). Conclusion: Atorvastatin was the most commonly utilized lipid-lowering drug. All prescribed monotherapies and combination regimens resulted in statistically significant improvements in lipid profiles, demonstrating effective therapeutic outcomes in routine clinical practice.
tags: Hyperlipidemia, Drug utilization pattern, Atorvastatin, Rosuvastatin, Fenofibrate, Statins, Combination therapy.
title: AN ANALYSIS OF THE DRUG UTILIZATION PATTERNS OBSERVED IN PATIENTS WITH HYPERLIPIDEMIA

summary: Agentic frameworks, software libraries that coordinate large language model calls, tool use, memory, and multi step reasoning into autonomous or semi autonomous workflows, have moved from research prototypes to production infrastructure within a span of roughly two years. Four frameworks have emerged as leading options for enterprise adoption: LangGraph, a graph based orchestration library built around explicit state machines, CrewAI, a role based framework that models agents as a crew of collaborating specialists, Strands Agents, a model driven software development kit that emphasizes minimal orchestration code, and watsonx Orchestrate, a managed enterprise platform built around prepackaged skills and governance tooling. Despite rapid adoption, there has been little independent, head to head measurement of how these frameworks compare on the dimensions that matter most to enterprise adopters: end to end latency, latency under concurrent load, cost per task, reliability and error recovery, and enterprise readiness characteristics such as security, observability, and governance. This article presents an empirical benchmark of all four frameworks against a common task suite spanning six task categories and three complexity tiers. We report latency percentiles, a stage level latency breakdown, concurrency scaling behavior, cost per task, task success rates, and a structured enterprise readiness score. We further document each framework's orchestration topology, developer experience characteristics, and security and governance posture, and we translate the results into a practical decision framework for selecting among the four frameworks under different enterprise constraints. All benchmark figures in this article are illustrative, reflecting a representative test harness and reference workload rather than any single vendor's published numbers, and are intended to demonstrate a repeatable evaluation method rather than a definitive ranking.
title: LANGGRAPH, CREWAI, STRANDS, OR WATSONX ORCHESTRATE? AN EMPIRICAL BENCHMARK OF AGENTIC FRAMEWORKS FOR ENTERPRISE READINESS AND LATENCY

summary: This repository provides the Python implementation of a self-supervised hybrid deep learning framework for lung CT image classification. The pipeline includes CT image preprocessing, SimCLR-based self-supervised learning, VGG16 and Swin Transformer feature extraction, attention-based feature fusion, PCA-based dimensionality reduction, and classification using XGBoost, Random Forest, and MLP. The repository also includes dataset preparation scripts, baseline comparisons, ablation experiments, evaluation metrics, explainable AI methods, configuration files, and implementation documentation. The framework is designed for binary classification of benign and malignant lung nodules using LIDC-IDRI and IQ-OTH/NCCD CT datasets.
tags: Lung Cancer, CT Images, SimCLR, VGG16, Swin Transformer, XGBoost, Deep Learning
title: A Self-Supervised Hybrid Pipeline for Robust and Interpretable Lung Cancer Classification from CT Scan Images — Source Code

summary: Chlorine-based disinfectants are standard for environmental-surface disinfection in healthcare facilities, yet their reaction with organic residues generates disinfection by-products (DBPs) whose occurrence, levels, and occupational relevance on hospital surfaces remain uncharacterized. Key gaps are the lack of a validated method and baseline data, the unresolved origin of surface N-nitrosamines, and the unknown influence of chlorine, temperature, humidity, and pre-cleaning on the surface DBP signal. We developed an isotope-dilution wipe-sampling, solid-phase extraction, and ultra-performance liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (UPLC-MS/MS) method for eight priority DBPs, applied it to 125 wipe samples from five departments across three campuses of a tertiary hospital in Wenzhou, and complemented field work with stainless-steel coupon experiments. Validation gave r ≥ 0.999, detection limits of 0.8–3.8 pg/cm², and recoveries of 78.4%–96.8%; field detection and quantification frequencies were 87.2% (95% CI 80.2–92.0%) and 69.6% (95% CI 61.1–77.0%), with operating rooms showing the highest total load (Kruskal–Wallis H(4) = 27.86, P < 0.001) though no pairwise contrast survived Bonferroni correction. In coupon experiments the net signal rose with chlorine and temperature but not humidity, with an unexplained chlorine-dependent increment (≈55% at 2000 mg/L) reflecting analytical signal behavior rather than verified formation chemistry, and pre-cleaning reduced haloacetic acids and chlorophenols by 35–55% but N-nitrosamines by only 3–9%. These results provide the first isotope-dilution baseline of DBP loads on healthcare surfaces, a reproducible monitoring method, and occurrence data for revising disinfection and occupational-hygiene standards, and they identify precursor-controlled formation experiments, biological monitoring, and direct testing of medical rubber as next steps.
tags: disinfection by-products; healthcare environmental surface; ultra-performance liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry; wipe sampling; N-nitrosamines; occupational exposure
title: Determination of Chlorination Disinfection By-products on Healthcare Environmental Surfaces by Ultra-Performance Liquid Chromatography–Tandem Mass Spectrometry

summary: Data Type: CSV, Experiment  Organized by: Research group of Shenzhen Research Institute, University of International Business and Economics, and a principal researcher from the University of Sassari, Italy  Approval ID: UIBE-4635876 The dataset contains 876 linked scene records representing 73 participants, each contributing responses to 12 virtual tourism presentations. Six destination settings are represented: a heritage courtyard, coastal promenade, forest trail, museum gallery, mountain lookout and historic street. Each setting has a LiDAR and a photogrammetric version, yielding 438 records per reconstruction condition. Each row identifies a participant, destination and reconstruction condition. The source CSV contains participant age and VR familiarity, presentation order, exposure duration, experiential ratings and technical descriptors. Experiential variables include psychological immersion, presence, perceived spatial coherence, emotional valence, arousal and workload. Technical variables include geometric error, texture ratings, frame rate, motion summaries and the interval between modality sessions. Neural features comprise 1,200 EEG values organised across 30 channels and 40 frequency bins spanning 1–40 Hz, together with 12 fMRI regional summaries. The regional labels cover bilateral dorsolateral prefrontal, precentral, postcentral, inferior parietal and superior parietal regions, plus ventromedial prefrontal cortex and precuneus. These values use arbitrary units and do not represent raw electrical waveforms or anatomically extracted BOLD measurements. The analysis CSV aggregates EEG frequency values into five bands: delta, theta, alpha, beta and gamma. This produces 150 EEG features per record. Combining these with the 12 regional summaries produces 162 neural predictors. Mean immersion combines the two session ratings; values of at least 4.5 define the high immersion category. The analysis file also contains participant validation fold assignments, held-out predictions and classifier scores. All records from a participant share the same validation fold. Prediction and score columns are analytical outputs and must be excluded from model inputs. Mean immersion is 4.59 for LiDAR and 3.95 for photogrammetry. Verified primary balanced accuracy is 81.97% for EEG, 79.66% for fMRI and 79.01% for the combined model.
title: Decoding Immersive VR Tourism: Reconstruction Quality and Neural Indicators of Immersion

summary: R scripts and aggregate tables that reproduce every number, table and figure in the article What a national health information system measures: a cross-sectional analysis of respiratory syncytial virus records in Bulgaria, 2022–2026 (Folia Medica, manuscript 215603) and its supplementary files. The package contains the reconstruction ledger of the Ministry of Health release of Bulgarian National Health Information System (NHIS) records for ICD-10 J21.0, J12.1, J20.5 and B97.4; exclusion and validation counts; the 110 distinct laboratory result values (109 text strings and the empty text field of numeric results) with their assigned RSV class and the rule that fired; a script that rebuilds the hospitalisation episodes from the released worksheet; annual population denominators at national and district level (National Statistical Institute table 206/649, population on 31 December 2022–2025); the aggregate model input (year × age × sex cases and person-years, with and without Sliven); model output and diagnostics; and the article figures. Aggregate data only. No record-level rows, identifiers or dates of birth are included; the record-level extract can be requested from the Bulgarian Ministry of Health under the Access to Public Information Act. See README.md for the file map, data sources, disclosure control and how to re-run the pipeline. Tables and figures: CC BY 4.0; R scripts: MIT licence.
title: Reproducibility package (R scripts and aggregate tables) for: What a national health information system measures: a cross-sectional analysis of respiratory syncytial virus records in Bulgaria, 2022–2026

summary: Source data, live Excel calculations, source-reference key and reproducible analysis code supporting Yield advantages and resource-reporting gaps in plant factories with artificial lighting. A meta-analysis . The curated workbook contains 784 plant-factory treatment records from 154 sources, with eligibility flags selecting 689 analyzed records from 125 sources. summary: This metadata entry record constitutes the fourth, concluding installment of a foundational cosmological paper tetralogy (complementing the preceding works registered under DOI:10.5281/zenodo.22763071, DOI:10.5281/zenodo.23153625, and DOI:10.5281/zenodo.23209528).  In this final paper, we formalize the self-consistent microphysical scenarios and underlying relativistic field equations governing primordial lepto- and baryogenesis within a strictly deterministic, parameter-free Extremal Quantum Black Hole (EQBH) cosmological bounce framework occurring immediately post-turnaround. summary: This dataset is associated with the paper titled “When LLM-Generated Refactorings Ripple: An Empirical Study of Repository Adoption Readiness”. The study examines whether LLM-generated refactorings of individual Java files are ready for adoption in the surrounding repository. Ten production files were selected from each of 15 open-source Java repositories (150 files) and refactored by five LLM configurations (Claude Opus 4.8, DeepSeek v4 Pro, Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview, GPT-5.5 and Qwen 3.6 Plus) under two generation conditions (a single prompt and a LangGraph-based multi-agent pipeline), yielding 1,500 generation attempts and 1,455 eligible refactoring candidates. Each candidate is assessed for contract/dependency risk, detected broken-caller evidence, a behavioural-equivalence indicator, targeted tests and adoption readiness. summary: English abstract Can an artificial agent have subjective experience while lacking unrestricted authority to replace its governing task objective? This paper treats that possibility as a distinct design and evaluation problem, termed the third case. It separates phenomenal consciousness, goal-directed behavior, operational competence, temporal continuity, and decision authority. The hypothetical case, a functionally testable candidate, and the evidence concerning experience are different descriptions. The prompt-issuer is an explicit role that may itself be occupied by a potentially experiencing executor under upstream constraints. The framework preserves the project-specific composition B-Core = A-Core ⊕ Purple Box/Present. A-Core denotes a potentially stateful, learning, multi-model cognitive and executive system; Purple is an undisclosed candidate addition with intended history-dependent causal effects. ESSENTIAL is a protected specification of constraints and revision authority, logically associated with A-Core. A targeted comparison with IDA, LIDA, adjustable autonomy, and existing agent controls, at the access levels stated in section 2.4, locates the proposal within established work. The contribution is a project-specific evaluation contract for externally governed, internally continuous execution, rather than a demonstrated new consciousness mechanism. Three limited analytical observations concern goal delegation, policy differences masked by a shared guard, and the gap between an architectural effect and consciousness. The proposed studies distinguish causal relevance from practical benefit, score feasible completion and justified infeasibility separately, and control initialization, history transfer, order, and dependent observations. No empirical result or proof of phenomenal consciousness is claimed. Functional findings could remain valuable if the consciousness hypothesis is rejected; credible welfare concerns would require assessment that task success alone cannot resolve. Magyar absztrakt Lehet-e egy mesterséges ágensnek szubjektív átélése úgy, hogy közben nincs korlátlan jogköre irányadó feladatcéljának lecserélésére? A tanulmány ezt a lehetőséget önálló tervezési és értékelési problémaként kezeli, és harmadik esetnek nevezi. Elkülöníti a fenomenális tudatosságot, a célirányos viselkedést, a működési kompetenciát, az időbeli folytonosságot és a döntési jogkört. A hipotetikus eset, a funkcionálisan vizsgálható jelölt és az átélésre vonatkozó bizonyíték eltérő leírások. A promptot kiadó szereplő kifejezetten meghatározott szerepet tölt be, amelyet maga is betölthet egy esetleg átéléssel rendelkező, a hierarchia felsőbb szintjéről korlátozott végrehajtó. A keretrendszer megőrzi a projektre jellemző B-Core = A-Core ⊕ Purple Box/Present összetételt. Az A-Core egy potenciálisan állapotos, tanuló, több modellt használó kognitív és végrehajtó rendszert jelöl; a Purple egy nem közölt felépítésű kiegészítőjelölt, amelynek előzményfüggő oksági hatásokat szánnak. Az ESSENTIAL a korlátok és a módosítási jogkör védett specifikációja, amely logikailag az A-Core-hoz kapcsolódik. Az IDA-val, a LIDA-val, az állítható autonómiával és az ágensek meglévő irány&i
title: The Third Case: Prompt-Governed Agency under a Consciousness Hypothesis

summary: Graduate students increasingly need publication literacy that combines scientific writing, research integrity, journal selection, and the ability to navigate peer review. This study profiled the understanding of reputable scientific article writing among students in a Master's Program in Sports Coaching Education and identified areas that require targeted academic support. The study used a descriptive quantitative design with total sampling. Forty-three active master's students completed a closed Likert-scale questionnaire after a scientific writing workshop. The instrument covered six domains: scientific article structure, the IMRaD system, publication ethics and plagiarism, reputable-journal selection, citation and referencing, and peer review and revision. Scores were converted into percentages using the procedure defined in the study protocol. The overall understanding score was 75.58%, which the progress report classified as "Good Understanding" because it remained below the 76% threshold for the highest category. Four comparatively weaker items were writing IMRaD sections according to scientific conventions (68.6%), identifying appropriate information for each IMRaD section (69.8%), responding appropriately to reviewer comments (70.1%), and distinguishing scientific articles from popular or opinion articles (71.8%). The findings indicate that students possess a relatively strong conceptual foundation but still need support in applied genre knowledge and publication-process skills. Writing clinics should therefore prioritize guided IMRaD practice, article deconstruction, simulated reviewer-response exercises, and structured journal-selection activities. Because the survey was administered after the workshop and no baseline measure was available, the results describe current understanding and do not establish workshop effectiveness.

summary: Code and results for the simulation study "Code and simulation results for: Do observable calibration metrics identify the best competing-risks prediction model? summary: The capabilities of an agent swarm depend on both its individual members and how they coordinate. Yet existing multi-agent systems often train agents within fixed orchestration structures, separating the learning of individual capabilities from the organization of collective behavior. We introduce market-based post-training (MPT), a framework for jointly learning action policies and self-orchestration in decentralized agent swarms. Agents express their willingness to participate through bids, which determine who acts and how collective outcomes provide local training credit. Learning both action and bidding behavior allows individual capabilities and patterns of participation to adapt together without a central coordinating agent. We evaluate MPT on embodied crafting, robot navigation, and deep research. Results show gains over monolithic post-training and confirm that agent participation indeed evolves with learning. With the same post-trained action policies, learned self-orchestration outperforms alternative coordination strategies. Ablations show that both action and bidding benefit from learning, and that learned bids provide more effective action-training signals. Beyond the original training objectives, trained swarms adapt faster to related tasks and achieve better performance with larger populations at inference time. Larger populations also suffer smaller performance losses under agent dropout, demonstrating that learned self-orchestration supports reuse, scaling, and robustness in decentralized agent swarms. Code and trained models are available at https://github.com/Embodied-Minds-Lab/MPT.

summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in multi-agent environments that produce unanimous agreement, both in intended interactions that need coordination and in unintended emergent interactions. Consequently, understanding how LLMs with competing incentives reach consensus is crucial to better interpret and design LLM collectives. We introduce an evaluation, based on the Network Consensus game, to assess the mechanisms driving this process. Here, a network of agents must agree on one of two colours to receive a payoff, but agents are offered different payoffs for the agreed colour. We vary components such as communication access and network structure and assess six open-source models and one closed model (ChatGPT 5.6-sol). We find that open-source LLMs reach consensus less often than humans in comparable experiments and only if messages are communicated across the global network. ChatGPT 5.6-sol, however, is able to reach consensus with communication limited to its neighbours and with no communication ability. This is achieved through lower stubbornness and higher majority-following tendencies, and by providing more information about its neighbours' states in messages. However, situating agents in a highly clustered graph reduces consensus, regardless of these traits, demonstrating that both system design and individual model traits drive collective outcomes.
title: Drivers of LLM Consensus Formation Under Competing Incentives: A Simulation Study

summary: Cooperative driving at mixed-traffic unsignalized intersections is challenged by imperfect vehicle-to-everything (V2X) communication, human-driven vehicle (HV) intentions that cannot be directly communicated, and the potential incompatibility of independently generated crossing decisions. This paper proposes State-Intent-Aware Graph Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Cooperative Driving under Imperfect V2X (SIGN-MAPPO) to address these challenges through three coordinated mechanisms. Each decision-eligible connected and automated vehicle (CAV) first reconstructs a receiver-specific traffic graph from its ego state and the peer-state records available to it, from which a shared graph-attention policy generates a raw Stop/Go intention augmented with predicted HV-intent features. CAV intentions are then exchanged through timestamped vehicle-to-vehicle (V2V) messages, and a local conflict-aware arbitration layer converts each CAV's intention into a safe executable action despite potentially inconsistent peer information. In the principal Simulation of Urban MObility (SUMO) evaluation, SIGN-MAPPO achieves a 97.53% completion rate, a 0.10% collision rate, and a mean intersection traversal time of 35.28 s. Ablation studies further confirm the complementary contributions of HV-intent prediction and CAV-intent exchange to this performance. The trained policy also remains robust under the evaluated communication-delay and packet-loss ranges, and cross-scenario tests show complete traffic clearance across the tested settings, though safety margins narrow under compound unpredictable HV behavior.
title: SIGN-MAPPO: State-Intent-Aware Graph Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Cooperative Driving under Imperfect V2X

summary: This paper studies parameter families of finite exponential sums in which two tie endpoints of a near-maximum level set approach at the critical rate δ_r ≍ qr^{-1/2}. The endpoint separation, half-bowl width, and competitor-kernel decay length then coincide. The cluster trio is rigid: its three exponents are determined by the level and endpoint positions, while coefficient ratios and other competitors require separate control. In a realized family, six rescaled kernels carry the interaction through one microscopic phase. Under explicit kernel-convergence hypotheses, the second-order term has a joint limit given by the excess sublevel length of a limiting profile, decomposed into a separated-endpoint sum and an interaction term. For an explicit four-term family, the hypotheses are verified with uniform explicit constants for every admissible phase lock. Two families have identical spectra and corresponding coefficient moduli at every radius but different critical limits. Along an unlocked calibration, phase dependence yields non-existence of the critical limit for specified parameters; certified intervals quantify the gap, and failure persists on an open parameter set. For a positive zero-lock family, upper and lower bounds describe the excluded shared arc. Full exclusion never occurs, and nonempty exclusion requires an additional parameter condition. The formal endpoint-anchored cap cannot be realized by a family satisfying the cluster hypotheses. High-precision numerical measurements on actual exponential sums compare with the profiles and exhibit phase dependence.
title: Critical-Scale Clustering and the Breakdown of Universality for Near-Maximum Phase Measures of Exponential Sums

summary: Artifact release v5.2 for the HTTP/1.1 case study Enabled Is Not Migrated: Moving Ongoing Traffic to Hybrid Post-Quantum TLS . This version preserves the v5.1 derived results and adds a claim-to-evidence map, measurement source, pinned dependency identities, configurations, setup guidance and six complete sanitized scientific run records. The raw examples cover lifetime check off, a 30-second lifetime and immediate replacement, locally and over the Internet. They use the lowest seed in each environment, steady traffic, and 20 ms added RTT for the Internet cases. Offline validation reconstructs their scientific reductions; the aggregate scripts reproduce four figures and the full derived comparisons. These six examples are not a full raw-campaign audit. Full raw records remain with the author and may be supplied in a later version if requested. No new experiment or capped-admission benefit is claimed. Deployment addresses and names are replaced by consistent symbols; a same-length Host substitution preserves byte lengths. Keys, credentials, executables, cloud administration records and manuscript/LaTeX source are excluded. Restrictions and provenance limits are documented. Files remain restricted for peer review and research reproducibility. Data/documentation use CC BY 4.0; original code uses MIT, with upstream NGINX terms retained for patch context.

summary: We consider the three-dimensional Prandtl boundary layer equations near a smooth structured solution (u_s, K u_s) with ∂z K ≡ 0. Under a monotone-or-degenerate profile assumption on u_s(·), we prove local well-posedness, continuous dependence, and a priori estimates in the critical Sobolev space X^s = H^s_γ(r) × H^s_γ(q) × H^s_γ(∇{x,y} q), where r = u − u_s and q = v − K u. Our proof does not assume smallness of the data, monotonicity of ∂_z u_s, or Gevrey regularity. We also establish a nonlinear norm-inflation result showing that the raw H^s topology on q alone is insufficient, and we identify the minimal tangential derivative of q required. Several stress tests, counterexamples, and open problems are discussed.
title: Sobolev Well-Posedness for Three-Dimensional Prandtl Boundary Layers Near Proportional Structures in a Critical Transverse Space

summary: Replication package for Legrenzi, Ciola and Bazzana, “Adaptation to climate-induced macrofinancial risks: top-down and bottom-up solutions”. The package contains the MATLAB implementation of a Stock-Flow-Consistent Agent-Based Integrated Assessment Model, the empirical calibration and the PSO/RWMH structural estimation routines, the input data on emissions and climate damages, the full simulation output (13 scenarios with 250 Monte Carlo simulations each), and the scripts that regenerate figures and tables in the paper. Running "master_replication.m" in the package root reproduces the complete set of exhibits. See "README.txt" for software requirements, folder structure and a file-by-file description.

summary: Post-Soviet states have spent three decades rebuilding the civic curriculum around national rather than supranational loyalties, yet claims that modernized patriotic education changes what students know and value seldom face controlled scrutiny. This study evaluates a convergent model that couples national heritage content with interactive methods, digital gamification, STEAM-linked projects, and the weekly Kelajak Soati (Future Hour) curriculum in Uzbek general secondary schools. A three-stage quasi-experiment (ascertaining, 2022-2023; formative, 2023-2024; summative, 2024-2025) enrolled 1,192 students in ten schools across Tashkent, Fergana, and Navoiy, allocated to experimental (n = 594) and control (n = 598) conditions. Groups were equivalent at baseline (M = 3.52 vs. 3.53 on a three-level scale scored 3-5; t = −0.12, p = .90; χ 2 (2) = 0.40, p = .82). At post-test the experimental group outperformed the control group (M = 3.92 vs. 3.52; Welch t(1184.4) = 10.46, p < .001, d = 0.61; χ 2 (2) = 141.78, Cramér’s V = .34), with non-overlapping 97% confidence intervals and an effectiveness ratio of 1.11. summary: This technical note documents a conditional mathematical correspondence between the static spatial kernel used in conventional electromagnetic potential theory and the fixed-source gravitational potential in Lisa Doumbouya’s Harmonic Physics programme. Under supplied three-dimensional Euclidean geometry, spherical symmetry and stated boundary conditions, the derivation gives the static Green function 1/(4πr). Applying the existing gravitational source normalization yields the potential −μ/r, whose radial derivative gives the inward acceleration −μ/r². The note distinguishes potential, field amplitude, intensity, acceleration and optical measurement conversion, keeping geometric normalization separate from the distance exponent. The optical phase-ruler results are reviewed alongside the GRACE-FO forward forecasts. Calibrated reconstruction using measured phase retained micrometre-scale agreement with processed microwave ranging, while some forward models produced much larger errors. These results do not establish exponential error growth or identify a unique physical cause. The correspondence uses established mathematics and remains conditional on the supplied geometry, source calibration and physical interpretation. It does not establish an electromagnetic mechanism of gravity or derive spatial geometry from foundational Phase. The note includes the analytical proof, assumptions, evidence boundaries and requirements for a subsequent physical test. No new experimental data are introduced.

summary: This working paper develops a relational Phase interpretation of black holes within the Harmonic Physics research programme, using general relativity, exact Kerr geometry and semiclassical black-hole thermodynamics as its physical baseline. It examines how phase organisation, temporal reference, observer accessibility and information persistence might relate to black-hole closure. Within the proposed framework, a phase-cycle is a closed relational structure that supports recurrence. Measured succession requires distinguishable relations and persistent records, while geometry and causal history are treated as observer-level reconstructions. The temporal-anchor hypothesis concerns a deeper terminal condition at which the parent domain loses the internally usable references needed to resolve further clocks and geometry. This proposed condition is kept distinct from the regular event horizon, across which local evolution continues. Observation is described through a joint observation relation among admitted source organisation, a physical channel and an observer-capable organisation. Source state, coupling and registered record retain separate roles; changes in accessibility may alter registration while the source organisation persists. The paper consolidates three bounded mathematical findings: exact Kerr ingoing and outgoing endpoints can have opposite trapped and anti-trapped orientations with the same mass and spin parameters; spherical source/exterior matching leaves the transition law undetermined; and a leading slow-rotation calculation permits the same sign of angular momentum in closing and opening configurations. These results establish compatibility within the stated geometric constructions. A physical transition mechanism remains to be derived. Black-to-white-hole models provide external theoretical comparisons. Return to the original exterior and the opening of a daughter phase are treated as distinct hypotheses, each requiring an appropriate causal structure, state map and conservation accounting. The remaining requirements include an invariant parent-relative terminal criterion, a physical Phase-to-boundary map, transition dynamics, information and entropy accounting, and a stable nonperturbative rotating completion. The paper remains a developing theoretical interpretation supported by standard-geometry comparisons and bounded symbolic checks. It does not establish a physical black-to-white transition, information recovery through evaporation or a daughter universe. Version 2.3, dated 17 October 2026, updates observation and self-nesting terminology, clarifies geodesic incompleteness and fixed-angular-momentum assumptions, and refreshes the references. The existing displayed equations and reported test results are retained. keywords: Phase Theory; black holes; event horizons; geodesic incompleteness; relational time; phase contraction; information accessibility; singularity; white holes; quantum gravity.
title: Black Holes as Temporal Anchors
