summary: We develop a regularized finite element method for the fractional conductivity equation, recovering the conductivity on an exterior observation region from noisy Dirichlet-to-Neumann measurements and using this reconstruction to determine the interior conductivity. Mesh-localized inputs and mass-lumped Tikhonov regularization discretize the exterior determination principle of Covi--Railo--Zimmermann (2026, Calc. Var. PDE). We prove exterior \(L^2\)- and \(L^\infty\)-convergence with error estimates, including the logarithmic correction at the critical Hölder exponent. The exterior reconstruction enables the Liouville reduction to the Calderón problem for the fractional Schrödinger equation. Separated measurements recover the interior potential, after which overlapping measurements determine the exterior potential tail. Together with the recovered exterior conductivity, the tail supplies the exterior Cauchy data for a Tikhonov-regularized finite element least-squares continuation. We prove \(H^s\)-convergence of the transformed conductivity and \(L^2\)-convergence of the interior conductivity, together with logarithmic state-bias and conductivity error estimates for full observation spaces. The admissible reconstructions remain uniformly positive and bounded. We present one- and two-dimensional numerical experiments illustrating the accuracy of the exterior and interior reconstructions and their sensitivity to measurement noise and discretization.
title: A finite element exterior-to-interior reconstruction in the fractional conductivity inverse problem

summary: We consider the inverse problem of recovering a potential $q$, depending on space and time, in the wave equation $(\Box_g+q)u=0$ on a Lorentzian manifold. We prove Lipschitz stability for a formally determined version of this problem under a \textit{null-cone foliation} assumption. As a consequence, we obtain uniqueness in the Lorentzian Calderón problem for $q$ under this assumption. Our approach is based on a modification of the Bukhgeim--Klibanov method using distorted plane waves.
title: Stability for a formally determined Lorentzian inverse problem

summary: A natural strategy for inverse problems with scarce labelled data is to transfer relational structure learned from abundant forward-simulation data. We show this strategy fails systematically, even when it satisfies the standard theoretical justification for why structure should help. We prove that approximate structure provides estimation-error benefits whenever the edge error satisfies $Δ< n^2 - kn$, reducing sample complexity from $O(n^2)$ to $O(kn+Δ)$. Structure learned via Neural Relational Inference (NRI) from dynamics prediction satisfies this condition, yet on a source-localisation task across 180 CFD-simulated hydrogen-leak scenarios and 180 acoustic scenarios, it degrades performance by 116% and 201% relative to a flexible, task-optimised attention baseline, while a physics-based prior (Green's function) degrades by only 69-72%. Four independent lines of evidence show this is not a tuning failure: NRI improves only 0.5% when given 18x more training data (versus 16.6% for the task-optimised baseline, $p<0.001$); performance is insensitive to the NRI edge threshold across a wide range; the dynamics-learned graph overlaps the task-optimal graph on only 6% of edges; and two further dynamics-derived structure estimators (correlation- and mutual-information-based) show no measurable benefit over a structure-free baseline, with the correlation-based estimator performing markedly worse. We formalise this gap as a statement about approximation error that the edge-accuracy condition cannot control, and we provide a lightweight transferability test (Jaccard similarity against a partially-observed target-task graph) that separates successful from failed transfer in all four domain/structure pairs we evaluate, using under an hour of computation and 15-20% of target-domain data; we present this as a heuristic calibrated on few cases, not a validated general threshold.
title: Edge Accuracy Is Not Enough: Why Dynamics-Learned Structure Fails to Transfer to Inverse Problems

summary: Split Gibbs sampling (SGS) is a popular framework for posterior sampling in Bayesian imaging inverse problems. It decouples a Gaussian data-fidelity term from a complex prior through an auxiliary variable, so the data variable is updated exactly and only the prior-side conditional is hard to sample. Existing samplers treat this conditional in one of two ways. Plug-and-play SGS runs a multi-step diffusion denoiser at every iteration, which is expensive and lacks non-asymptotic guarantees. Langevin-within-SGS takes cheap overdamped Langevin steps but needs many iterations. We propose RED-KLwSGS, which keeps the exact Gaussian update for the data variable and updates the auxiliary variable with underdamped (kinetic) Langevin diffusions driven by a one-shot denoising score, at the same per-iteration cost as Langevin-within-SGS. We prove non-asymptotic Wasserstein-2 convergence in continuous and discrete time for strongly log-concave priors. We also introduce Joint-RED-KLwSGS, which applies kinetic Langevin diffusions to both variables. Experiments with Denoising diffusion probabilistic models as diffusion priors on FFHQ and ImageNet datasets show faster convergence and high-quality image reconstruction.
title: Kinetic Langevin Meets Split Gibbs: Accelerated Posterior Sampling for Imaging Inverse Problems with Diffusion Priors

summary: This study aims to improve the directional sensitivity of magnetic resonance hydrophone (MRH) methods and allow for detection and quantification of waves traveling at any angle relative to the MRI bore-axis. Doing so may better integrate MRH technology into transcranial focused ultrasound neuromodulation therapies. Existing MRH implementations only encode acoustic waves propagating along the MRI bore-axis, precluding use with wide aperture transducers or temporal skull windows. This study expands the MRH technique into a MR-based Omni-directional Hydrophone (MRbOH) that can quantify the magnitude pressure and phase of waves propagating at any angle. The MRbOH method formulates a system of equations around uniquely sensitized images that, when solved, introduce sensitivity to oblique acoustic waves. The method was tested experimentally in a gel phantom that was insonated at $0^o$, $45^o$, and $90^o$ relative to the MRI bore-axis. The method reconstructed pressure maps at all three angles of propagation, including features such as peak pressure, partial reflections, and beamwidth. The MRbOH method measured an average beamwidth of 16.2 mm while the hydrophone measured a beamwidth of 14.5 mm. Average hydrophone-measured pressure within a region of interest was 416.19 $\boldsymbol{\pm}$ 78.07 kPa. Average MRbOH measured pressure in the same region at $0^o$, $45^o$, and $90^o$, respectively, were: 285.5 $\boldsymbol{\pm}$ 49.5 kPa, 193.13 $\boldsymbol{\pm}$ 43.55 kPa, 194.7 $\boldsymbol{\pm}$ 47.38 kPa. In addition, the study presents and experimentally verifies a statistical noise model that predicted the mean with $R^2 = 0.85$, and standard deviation with $R^2 = 0.83$.
title: The Magnetic-Resonance-Based, Omni-Directional Hydrophone

summary: The individual attribution of sperm whale (Physeter macrocephalus) vocalizations during surface interactions constitutes a methodological challenge due to acoustic overlaps, multipath propagation, body shadowing, and indistinguishable inter-pulse intervals among similar-sized individuals. A multimodal audio-visual workflow is presented to deinterleave and attribute uncharacterized click trains produced by immature males during ``vocal sparring'' using a portable three-hydrophone array coupled with synchronized video. The approach combines spectro-temporal tracking, based on inter-click interval dynamics and the Constant-Q Transform, with spatial time-difference-of-arrival modeling projected onto the image plane for optical validation. Analysis of 2,655 manually validated clicks shows that purely acoustic clustering diarization errors remain low, peaking at 25.79% only during extreme temporal superpositions. Integrating the optical modality resolves residual spatial indeterminacies; although near-planar array geometry induces vertical ambiguities, the system achieves up to 100% horizontal visual concordance for primary emitters. Crucially, this framework successfully reconstructed and assigned 11 distinct, intertwined click trains totaling 882 clicks to specific focal individuals despite near-field tactile constraints. Because ethological descriptions remain incomplete without identifying the emitter, explicitly correlating these emissions with physical kinematics provides the fine-scale resolution required to define this socio-acoustic behavior.
title: Audiovisual diarization of overlapping click trains in sperm whale (Physeter macrocephalus) vocal sparring using a three-hydrophone array

summary: Advances in computational methods have made full-wave simulations in large disordered media increasingly feasible, but the resulting volume of field data, scaling with the cube of the ratio of system size to wavelength, creates a severe storage and post-processing bottleneck. Generic compression methods are sample-specific and preclude operations on compressed data. We introduce OSCAR, a physics-based lossy compression scheme for monochromatic wave fields in weakly scattering media. OSCAR exploits the universal confinement of the Fourier representation of wave fields to a thin dispersion shell, a direct consequence of wave propagation when the scattering mean free path significantly exceeds the wavelength, and a property of every disorder realization rather than of the ensemble average, so that one mask serves an entire ensemble. The resulting compression ratio reflects two distinct scale separations: on-shell confinement due to weak scattering, and the excess Fourier-space volume introduced by sub-wavelength discretization of the scatterers. Crucially, second-order quantities, demonstrated here on sensitivity maps, can be computed via convolution entirely in compressed space while preserving the interference effects. We validate the method in 2D scalar and 3D vector simulations of electromagnetic waves, spanning quasi-ballistic to diffusive transport. The reconstruction error is set by the discarded spectral weight. Demonstrated compression ratios reach ~810x in 2D and ~420x in 3D at a 3% error, with cell-averaged second-order observables accurate to an even smaller error. Tested from quasi-ballistic to diffusive transport, OSCAR stores the fields in up to 19x less space at a 2.5-4.2x lower runtime cost than SZ3. This lowers the storage barrier to ensemble studies at scales relevant to biomedical optics, seismology, and underwater acoustics.
title: On-shell compression and reconstruction (OSCAR) of monochromatic wave fields in weakly scattering media

summary: Physics-informed machine learning has gained significant attention in recent years. In regimes of limited data, parametrized Gaussian processes have become popular. Existing approaches, however, often face limitations, such as requiring parametrizable (also called controllable) systems or a large number of output tasks. In this work, we introduce a systematic procedure we call "ghost tasking", using auxiliary tasks to circumvent these limitations. We prove that such ghost tasks can render any non-parametrizable system effectively parametrizable, enabling algorithmic construction of parametrized Gaussian Processes while keeping the number of required tasks (i.e. output dimensions) and latent functions low. We find that ghost tasking performs especially well in an inverse problem setting, even with very few available data. We show the usage and power of ghost tasking in three experiments, providing systematic comparisons to the only other currently available method applicable to all experiments. We provide necessary syntax and explications for two computer algebra programs that compute parametrizations for systems with polynomial or rational coefficients. Our theoretical results extend to systems with meromorphic functions.
title: Ghost tasking for parametrized Gaussian Processes solving linear differential equations

summary: Solutions to geophysical inverse problems are generally non-unique, and greatly benefit from additional geological prior information. Generative Neural Networks (GNNs) are commonly used to parametrise such information, typically restricting solutions to a lower-dimensional latent space. The final inversion result is obtained by mapping the latent space parameters to the original higher-dimensional model space using the GNNs. However, solutions then remain confined to a low-dimensional geological generative manifold; if the true Earth model lies outside of this manifold, standard latent space inversion fails. We propose a Bayesian model space inversion method that uses the generative manifold as a guide to find the solutions that lie outside this manifold. We validate our approach in non-linear travel-time tomography experiments on both simple and more geological structures. By comparing our method with model space inversion using uniform prior probabilities and standard latent-space inversion, we demonstrate that the less informative uniform prior fails to constrain the solution, while the latent space approach fails when the true Earth model lies outside of the generative manifold. Conversely, our new model-space inversion method successfully recovers complex off-manifold geological features while maintaining low solution uncertainty.
title: Escaping Geological Generative Prior Distributions in Bayesian Travel Time Tomography

summary: We study the relation between equal-weight circle quadrature, Gauss--Chebyshev quadrature, and planar Minkowski reconstruction. The regular $N$-point grid is an $\mathbb S^1$-design of strength $N-1$; a half-step rotation of the $2M$-point grid projects to the classical $M$-point Gauss--Chebyshev rule. A common family of quadrature-error functionals gives exact identities for integration error, mixed-area error, and support-function error. For $N\ge3$, the centered Minkowski polygon $P_N$ with perimeter $2π$ has the exact Hausdorff distance from the unit disk $B^2$ \[ d_H(P_N,B^2)=1-\fracπ{N}\cot\fracπ{N} =\frac{π^2}{3N^2}+O(N^{-4}). \] With Steiner centering, we obtain $d_H(K_μ,K_ν)\leπW_1(μ,ν)$ for balanced, nondegenerate probability measures, where $W_1$ uses geodesic distance. Its exponent is sharp even for smooth positive densities near the uniform measure. The identity $W_1(ν_N,σ)=π/(2N)$ yields a general $O(N^{-1})$ bound for the regular grid. The sharper $O(N^{-2})$ rate follows from the sparse discrepancy spectrum and the inverse multiplier $(1-k^2)^{-1}$. Finally, a perturbation estimate gives sufficient conditions for preserving the quadratic rate and its leading constant.
title: Gauss--Chebyshev Quadrature, $\mathbb S^1$-Designs, and the Planar Minkowski Inverse Problem: A One-Dimensional Model for Design-Induced Convex Geometry

summary: We consider the inverse problem of recovering time-dependent coefficients in a system of Schrödinger equations with coupled nonlinear terms. We first address the well-posedness of the system for small boundary data and trivial initial data. Then, we show that the linearized Neumann data stably determines the nonlinear coefficients provided that, at any given time, they are known in some neighborhood of the boundary. The proof relies on linearization and complex geometric optics (CGO) solutions for the linear Schrödinger equation. We conclude by outlining an approach based on the direct use of Carleman estimates to recover time-independent coefficients in the setting of trivial boundary data but nontrivial initial data.
title: Recovery of coefficients in a Schrödinger system with nonlinear coupling

summary: The logistic smooth-to-hard shrinker is the proximal map of an explicit saturating spectral penalty for general linear inverse problems. Its exact weak convexity yields a unique scaled update and proximal-gradient stationarity guarantees, while independent validation provides finite-grid parameter-selection control. We use MRI as an illustrative example.
title: Data-driven Smooth-to-hard Spectral Regularization for General Linear Inverse Problems

summary: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) can participate in producing educational research data as well as analysing them. This dual role creates opportunities for studying intellectual activity while complicating the relationship between observation and intervention. This conceptual article connects two research routes: analysis of existing narrative documents and study of trajectories produced through human–AI interaction. A selective historical genealogy links scientific photography, personal documents, concept mapping and verbal protocols to contemporary hybrid intelligence and learning analytics. Observable cognition denotes recorded manifestations of intellectual activity, interpreted under explicit conditions. Multiscale narrative analysis connects events, episodes, trajectories and corpora through within-case interpretation, cross-case comparison and return to original evidence. The central proposal is to preserve a revisable link between each cross-case claim, its supporting episodes, the provenance of contributions and evidence that could challenge the interpretation. The framework extends from conversational generative interaction to increasingly agentic configurations, in which greater trace granularity also increases the need to attribute operations to the human participant, the system, or distributed activity between them. The framework specifies data units, audit procedures and four propositions for empirical evaluation. A fictional educational design episode illustrates how the same revision can support competing explanations. The proposed tests separate the informational value of process records from claims about learning gains, and assess whether assisted analysis preserves consequential context at an acceptable cost. The framework integrates established methods into an assessable research design; its feasibility and comparative advantage remain to be demonstrated. -------- Preprint v1.0. This version has not undergone peer review.
title: From tacit knowledge to observable cognition: A framework for tracing interaction with AI and analysing educational narratives across scales

summary: This metadata entry record constitutes the fourth, concluding installment of a foundational cosmological paper tetralogy (complementing the preceding works registered under DOI:10.5281/zenodo.22763071, DOI:10.5281/zenodo.23153625, and DOI:10.5281/zenodo.23209528).  In this final paper, we formalize the self-consistent microphysical scenarios and underlying relativistic field equations governing primordial lepto- and baryogenesis within a strictly deterministic, parameter-free Extremal Quantum Black Hole (EQBH) cosmological bounce framework occurring immediately post-turnaround. Operating within the rigid geometric boundaries of an effective N=1 supergravity (SUGRA) action and a q-deformed U_q(su(2)) horizon algebra, we trace the top-down reverse-engineering map from Planck-scale remnants to Standard Model matter fields without invoking highly tuned auxiliary fields or unconstrained post-bounce inflation boundaries. Crucially, this work resolves the long-standing flavor puzzle within the ansatz by introducing a top-down, two-stage Inverse Spin-Seesaw cascade for the charged lepton sector. We demonstrate that below the Riemann-regularized zero-spin vacuum threshold (M_crit ≈ 0.5601 M_P), where both the asymptotic selectron and electron states obey the unshifted Casimir spin-algebraic relation, the discrete spin mismatch (ΔJ = √3/2) structurally locks the effective Yukawa coupling. This mechanism dynamically projects the heavy Planck-scale scalar selectron mass gap (M_e ≈ 0.002584 M_P) down to the Standard Model electron mass scale (m_e ≈ 0.511 MeV) via a single low-energy electroweak parameter (v_EW = 246.22 GeV), completely stripping the low-energy lepton flavor sector of arbitrary, adjustable inputs. Concurrently, the paper maps out: 1. Unified Lepto- and Baryogenesis Dynamics: Tracing the sub-Planckian three-body beta decays of dark-sector super-neutrons that seed the primary lepton background and active neutrino mass scales (m_nu_a ≈ 0.05 eV, m_nu_s ≈ 0.009 eV), paired with a laser-driven CP-violation mechanism that secures the observed baryon asymmetry. 2. Dual-Component Super-Atomic Dark Matter: Formalizing the freeze-out of unreacted sub-Planckian defects into single-charge ionic [M_0,0 x e]^- configurations regulated by an internal Coulomb blockade, and saturated neutral [M_0,0 x Nν] sneutrino super-atoms bounded by the strict Kaup-Ruffini-Bonazzola mass limit (M_max ≈ 0.29 g). This multi-component partitioning naturally resolves the empirical dark sector allocations (Ω_Λ ≈ 68.3%, Ω_c ≈ 26.9%). 3. Definitive Empirical Signatures: Providing explicit mappings onto next-generation polarization surveys, including a monochromatic microwave laser chirp (ν_now ≈ 1.5 GHz) that naturally matches the ARCADE 2 cosmic radio excess, and a sub-kilohertz wide-bandwidth stochastic gravitational wave noise background centered at 310.3 Hz. As the definitive structural synthesis of the entire tetralogy, this concluding work establishes a unified cosmological paradigm that is fundamentally parameter-free, independent of localized baryon asymmetry signs, and structurally renormalizable across varying deep ultraviolet scales.

summary: The capabilities of an agent swarm depend on both its individual members and how they coordinate. Yet existing multi-agent systems often train agents within fixed orchestration structures, separating the learning of individual capabilities from the organization of collective behavior. We introduce market-based post-training (MPT), a framework for jointly learning action policies and self-orchestration in decentralized agent swarms. Agents express their willingness to participate through bids, which determine who acts and how collective outcomes provide local training credit. Learning both action and bidding behavior allows individual capabilities and patterns of participation to adapt together without a central coordinating agent. We evaluate MPT on embodied crafting, robot navigation, and deep research. Results show gains over monolithic post-training and confirm that agent participation indeed evolves with learning. With the same post-trained action policies, learned self-orchestration outperforms alternative coordination strategies. Ablations show that both action and bidding benefit from learning, and that learned bids provide more effective action-training signals. Beyond the original training objectives, trained swarms adapt faster to related tasks and achieve better performance with larger populations at inference time. Larger populations also suffer smaller performance losses under agent dropout, demonstrating that learned self-orchestration supports reuse, scaling, and robustness in decentralized agent swarms. Code and trained models are available at https://github.com/Embodied-Minds-Lab/MPT.
title: Learning Self-Orchestration in Decentralized Agent Swarms

summary: Cooperative driving at mixed-traffic unsignalized intersections is challenged by imperfect vehicle-to-everything (V2X) communication, human-driven vehicle (HV) intentions that cannot be directly communicated, and the potential incompatibility of independently generated crossing decisions. This paper proposes State-Intent-Aware Graph Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Cooperative Driving under Imperfect V2X (SIGN-MAPPO) to address these challenges through three coordinated mechanisms. Each decision-eligible connected and automated vehicle (CAV) first reconstructs a receiver-specific traffic graph from its ego state and the peer-state records available to it, from which a shared graph-attention policy generates a raw Stop/Go intention augmented with predicted HV-intent features. CAV intentions are then exchanged through timestamped vehicle-to-vehicle (V2V) messages, and a local conflict-aware arbitration layer converts each CAV's intention into a safe executable action despite potentially inconsistent peer information. In the principal Simulation of Urban MObility (SUMO) evaluation, SIGN-MAPPO achieves a 97.53% completion rate, a 0.10% collision rate, and a mean intersection traversal time of 35.28 s. Ablation studies further confirm the complementary contributions of HV-intent prediction and CAV-intent exchange to this performance. The trained policy also remains robust under the evaluated communication-delay and packet-loss ranges, and cross-scenario tests show complete traffic clearance across the tested settings, though safety margins narrow under compound unpredictable HV behavior.
title: SIGN-MAPPO: State-Intent-Aware Graph Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Cooperative Driving under Imperfect V2X

summary: This paper studies parameter families of finite exponential sums in which two tie endpoints of a near-maximum level set approach at the critical rate δ_r ≍ qr^{-1/2}. The endpoint separation, half-bowl width, and competitor-kernel decay length then coincide. The cluster trio is rigid: its three exponents are determined by the level and endpoint positions, while coefficient ratios and other competitors require separate control. In a realized family, six rescaled kernels carry the interaction through one microscopic phase. Under explicit kernel-convergence hypotheses, the second-order term has a joint limit given by the excess sublevel length of a limiting profile, decomposed into a separated-endpoint sum and an interaction term. For an explicit four-term family, the hypotheses are verified with uniform explicit constants for every admissible phase lock. Two families have identical spectra and corresponding coefficient moduli at every radius but different critical limits. Along an unlocked calibration, phase dependence yields non-existence of the critical limit for specified parameters; certified intervals quantify the gap, and failure persists on an open parameter set. For a positive zero-lock family, upper and lower bounds describe the excluded shared arc. Full exclusion never occurs, and nonempty exclusion requires an additional parameter condition. The formal endpoint-anchored cap cannot be realized by a family satisfying the cluster hypotheses. High-precision numerical measurements on actual exponential sums compare with the profiles and exhibit phase dependence.
title: Critical-Scale Clustering and the Breakdown of Universality for Near-Maximum Phase Measures of Exponential Sums

summary: We consider the three-dimensional Prandtl boundary layer equations near a smooth structured solution (u_s, K u_s) with ∂z K ≡ 0. Under a monotone-or-degenerate profile assumption on u_s(·), we prove local well-posedness, continuous dependence, and a priori estimates in the critical Sobolev space X^s = H^s_γ(r) × H^s_γ(q) × H^s_γ(∇{x,y} q), where r = u − u_s and q = v − K u. Our proof does not assume smallness of the data, monotonicity of ∂_z u_s, or Gevrey regularity. We also establish a nonlinear norm-inflation result showing that the raw H^s topology on q alone is insufficient, and we identify the minimal tangential derivative of q required. Several stress tests, counterexamples, and open problems are discussed.
title: Sobolev Well-Posedness for Three-Dimensional Prandtl Boundary Layers Near Proportional Structures in a Critical Transverse Space

summary: Post-Soviet states have spent three decades rebuilding the civic curriculum around national rather than supranational loyalties, yet claims that modernized patriotic education changes what students know and value seldom face controlled scrutiny. This study evaluates a convergent model that couples national heritage content with interactive methods, digital gamification, STEAM-linked projects, and the weekly Kelajak Soati (Future Hour) curriculum in Uzbek general secondary schools. A three-stage quasi-experiment (ascertaining, 2022-2023; formative, 2023-2024; summative, 2024-2025) enrolled 1,192 students in ten schools across Tashkent, Fergana, and Navoiy, allocated to experimental (n = 594) and control (n = 598) conditions. Groups were equivalent at baseline (M = 3.52 vs. 3.53 on a three-level scale scored 3-5; t = −0.12, p = .90; χ 2 (2) = 0.40, p = .82). At post-test the experimental group outperformed the control group (M = 3.92 vs. 3.52; Welch t(1184.4) = 10.46, p < .001, d = 0.61; χ 2 (2) = 141.78, Cramér’s V = .34), with non-overlapping 97% confidence intervals and an effectiveness ratio of 1.11. Change concentrated at the lower threshold: the share of experimental students at the Low level fell from 58.4% to 23.9% while the Medium level rose from 30.8% to 60.6%; the control distribution did not move. Effects replicated in every region (d = 0.56-0.65), and net-of-baseline gains were as large in the rural Fergana district as in Navoiy. The model reliably converts civic disengagement into baseline civic literacy; whether it fosters constructive rather than conformist attachment remains untested. Implications for national scale-up and its evaluation are discussed.
title: HERITAGE, TECHNOLOGY, AND CIVIC ATTACHMENT: A THREE-REGION QUASI-EXPERIMENTAL EVALUATION OF CONVERGENT PATRIOTIC EDUCATION IN UZBEK SECONDARY SCHOOLS, 2022-2025

summary: This technical note documents a conditional mathematical correspondence between the static spatial kernel used in conventional electromagnetic potential theory and the fixed-source gravitational potential in Lisa Doumbouya’s Harmonic Physics programme. Under supplied three-dimensional Euclidean geometry, spherical symmetry and stated boundary conditions, the derivation gives the static Green function 1/(4πr). Applying the existing gravitational source normalization yields the potential −μ/r, whose radial derivative gives the inward acceleration −μ/r². The note distinguishes potential, field amplitude, intensity, acceleration and optical measurement conversion, keeping geometric normalization separate from the distance exponent. The optical phase-ruler results are reviewed alongside the GRACE-FO forward forecasts. Calibrated reconstruction using measured phase retained micrometre-scale agreement with processed microwave ranging, while some forward models produced much larger errors. These results do not establish exponential error growth or identify a unique physical cause. The correspondence uses established mathematics and remains conditional on the supplied geometry, source calibration and physical interpretation. It does not establish an electromagnetic mechanism of gravity or derive spatial geometry from foundational Phase. The note includes the analytical proof, assumptions, evidence boundaries and requirements for a subsequent physical test. No new experimental data are introduced.
title: Inverse Radius Kernel and Optical Phase Registration

The record contains a proposed claim-level review codebook for the Provenance-Controlled Cross-Lingual Audit Framework (PCAF), covering the unit of analysis, claim families (O/R/N/E), transformation layers (L1-L5), material alternatives, evidence and diagnostic dispositions, claim narrowing, and an independent-evaluation protocol, together with a blank audit register (CSV header only). These are proposed research instruments: they have not been validated, no independent coding study has been completed, and the CSV contains no data.
title: PCAF claim-level review codebook and blank audit register (v1.0)

summary: This working paper develops a relational Phase interpretation of black holes within the Harmonic Physics research programme, using general relativity, exact Kerr geometry and semiclassical black-hole thermodynamics as its physical baseline. It examines how phase organisation, temporal reference, observer accessibility and information persistence might relate to black-hole closure. Within the proposed framework, a phase-cycle is a closed relational structure that supports recurrence. Measured succession requires distinguishable relations and persistent records, while geometry and causal history are treated as observer-level reconstructions. The temporal-anchor hypothesis concerns a deeper terminal condition at which the parent domain loses the internally usable references needed to resolve further clocks and geometry. This proposed condition is kept distinct from the regular event horizon, across which local evolution continues. Observation is described through a joint observation relation among admitted source organisation, a physical channel and an observer-capable organisation. Source state, coupling and registered record retain separate roles; changes in accessibility may alter registration while the source organisation persists. The paper consolidates three bounded mathematical findings: exact Kerr ingoing and outgoing endpoints can have opposite trapped and anti-trapped orientations with the same mass and spin parameters; spherical source/exterior matching leaves the transition law undetermined; and a leading slow-rotation calculation permits the same sign of angular momentum in closing and opening configurations. These results establish compatibility within the stated geometric constructions. A physical transition mechanism remains to be derived. Black-to-white-hole models provide external theoretical comparisons. Return to the original exterior and the opening of a daughter phase are treated as distinct hypotheses, each requiring an appropriate causal structure, state map and conservation accounting. The remaining requirements include an invariant parent-relative terminal criterion, a physical Phase-to-boundary map, transition dynamics, information and entropy accounting, and a stable nonperturbative rotating completion. The paper remains a developing theoretical interpretation supported by standard-geometry comparisons and bounded symbolic checks. It does not establish a physical black-to-white transition, information recovery through evaporation or a daughter universe. Version 2.3, dated 17 October 2026, updates observation and self-nesting terminology, clarifies geodesic incompleteness and fixed-angular-momentum assumptions, and refreshes the references. The existing displayed equations and reported test results are retained. keywords: Phase Theory; black holes; event horizons; geodesic incompleteness; relational time; phase contraction; information accessibility; singularity; white holes; quantum gravity.
title: Black Holes as Temporal Anchors

summary: The mass gap and confinement problems of four-dimensional quantum Yang–Mills theory are solved by the exact duality between the continuous, scale-free Hamiltonian gauge field and the discrete, non-Hamiltonian vorton basis: 1. Continuous classical Yang–Mills theory is incomplete because the non-Abelian turbulent cascade drives energy to the microscale a, where phase-space volume contraction forces condensation into discrete vorton dipoles. 2. The core scale a = Lmax(Ncαs)^3/4 is generated dynamically by the termination of the Kolmogorov cascade. 3. The mass gap ∆YM =ℏcaκ1 is generated by the spontaneous mass permutation algebra of the Weyl group W(SU(Nc)) =∼ SNc operating on the tight horn torus geometry. 4. Color confinement follows from center-flux piercing statistics, establishing an area law with string tension σ > 0. This establishes a constructive, self-contained solution to the Clay Millennium problem in pure Yang–Mills theory.
title: Duality Between Classical Hamiltonian Yang–Mills Theory and the Non-Hamiltonian Vorton Basis: Spontaneous Mass Permutation at the Vorton Core

summary: This presentation offers a term for a harm that Ethnic Studies practitioners experience constantly and lack precise language for. It argues that the imprecision is itself a barrier to defense. Burnout is a convenient diagnostic category. It implies depletion from overwork, prescribes rest and strong boundaries, and locates the site of intervention in the self rather than the structure. This presentation argues that burnout functions as an institutional alibi. It recodes structural and relational injury as personal misalignment, and in doing so stabilizes the institution. Drawing on Foucault, the presentation shows how wellness discourse extends disciplinary power: workers become responsible for optimizing their own resilience within environments that remain unchanged. Burnout presumes excess. But what if the harm is not overextension but deprivation? Feminist ethics of care holds that care is a relational practice requiring response-ability. Without reciprocity, care becomes extraction. The presentation develops racialized relational starvation to name the chronic absence of reciprocal recognition, sponsorship, and institutional buffering in environments that nonetheless demand sustained care labor and loyalty. Asymmetry itself is not the injury. Fields are never flat. The distinction is between fluid asymmetry, where those holding institutional capital absorb risk and redistribute strain, and calcified asymmetry, where circulation stops and protection flows predictably in one direction. Stagnation is the greater harm, not simply hierarchy. Under these conditions, Ethnic Studies practitioners adapt through contortion: institutionally induced self-surveillance and anticipatory compliance, routinely misrecognized as professionalism and praised as diplomacy, composure, and reasonableness. The praise confirms the adaptation and leaves the conditions untouched. Sustained, contortion produces professional death, the cumulative erosion of ethical agency, epistemic confidence, relational participation, and pedagogical integrity, without formal departure. Those living it are the walking dead, structurally embedded, outwardly functioning, internally disengaged from the institution’s moral claims. Their continued presence lets the institution read survival as health. This is spirit murder in professional form, in the sense theorized by Love. It is not spectacle, but sediment, laid down through repetition. The presentation closes with a refusal of premature closure. It offers no reforms. To move quickly to prescription would rehabilitate the institution before the harm has been accounted for, converting accumulated injury into a problem of implementation. Where harm has been normalized and rendered ethically unintelligible, naming is not a step toward intervention. It is intervention. This is what a loving defense requires: the willingness to stay with what is happening long enough to name it precisely, and to refuse the comfort of solutions offered too soon. The presentation will be a twenty-minute talk with slides, moving through misnaming, starvation, contortion, and professional death, with the final minutes reserved for discussion. The vocabulary is offered as analytical scaffolding, and is only useful if others can test it against their own conditions and experiences.
title: Contortion Is Not Burnout: Racialized Relational Starvation and Professional Death in Ethnic Studies Work

summary: SELF-CALIBRATING NANO-NEURAL INTERFACES AND REFERENCE LINEAGE AT THE LIMIT Built-In References × Drift Attribution × Independent Functional Requalification STARLI / Institute XXIII / Research Flagship 17 PUBLICATION DESCRIPTION When a long-running neural interface changes, is the cause the sensor, the surrounding tissue, or the decoder? An adaptive algorithm can restore predictive accuracy while obscuring the physical origin of its own correction. This book proposes a rigorous, falsifiable architecture for self-calibrating nano-neural interfaces that must retain the scientific history of every reference and every update. Its central axiom is that self-calibration does not imply self-certification: measurement claims, permission to change, electrode safety and functional benefit demand independent evidence. The first coupling is the existence of physically traceable internal references that can be challenged against electrically and temporally independent standards. The second is a source-aware drift-diagnostic process that distinguishes electronics gain, electrode-tissue transfer, tissue-like surrogate changes, changing source signals and model/feature drift, explicitly recording instances of nonidentifiability. The third is external functional requalification, which can reject an apparently successful update after hidden-domain testing, material or reference replacement, loss of selectivity, missing raw observations, or inability to reproduce the frozen predecessor. This research monograph is divided into seven causal layers and 82 chapters. Five major subsections of each chapter are assigned independent pages, yielding 410 separately paginated technical essays. Thirty gold mathematical derivations are linked from chapter-opening equations to discriminating experiments. The mathematics includes augmented state-space observability, nonlinear observation functions, source-separation Jacobians, Kalman innovations, impedance spectroscopy, covariance propagation, change-point statistics, conformal coverage, selective risk, hard-veto constrained update eligibility, reference-bridge covariance, exact rollback and cross-laboratory requalification. A displayed formula is a candidate analytical instrument with stated dimensions and assumptions, not a discovered biological law. Two hundred detailed Research Gates are preserved at the rear: 82 interrogate source identifiability, another 82 challenge independent physical and evidential hard vetoes, and 36 require third-party reconstruction of a frozen reference history. Thirty-three Phoenix Answer Embryos propose revisable architectures, beginning with the Neural Interface Calibration Passport. The Passport ties an interface's physical identity to the raw analog and digitized record, calibrated unit chain, hardware reference ancestors, model and feature checksums, reasons for changing any reference, failed updates, revoked permissions, blinded requalification and rollback. These are proposed evidence structures, not commercially validated devices. The DOI bibliography contains 18 unique external research records covering chronic intracortical signal instability, low-dimensional BCI stabilization, decoder adaptation, long-term electrode-tissue behavior, complex impedance metrology, electrochemical reference limits, neural interface materials and conformal uncertainty under covariate shift. Selected publisher and PubMed pages were consulted for source metadata. Their findings cannot establish efficacy of the new self-calibration architecture; source-specific claims and independent replication would be necessary.

summary: This archive is the computational supplement for the manuscript “A five-qubit 1-resistant graph state and stabilizer marginal certificates” by Zicheng Han, Wanchen Zhang, and Xiande Zhang. It provides an exhaustive certificate-based classification of graph-state m-resistance for every connected local-Clifford (LC) class with N=5,...,11 vertices. One representative of each Danielsen LC class is included. For every representative, all admissible values m=0,...,N−2 are classified. For k=N−m−1, a graph state is accepted as m-resistant only when every k-vertex marginal has an explicit full-separability certificate and every (k+1)-vertex marginal has an explicit negative-partial-transpose (NPT) entanglement certificate. NPT certificates are obtained from exact integer Walsh spectra of partial transposes; no floating-point tolerance or analytical shortcut is used. The archive contains: - a self-contained Python classifier using only the Python standard library; - parsed representatives of all connected Danielsen LC classes for N=5,...,11; - one complete certificate record for every Danielsen class; - a decisive obstruction for every failed graph/m pair; - compact per-class and per-(N,m) summary tables; - provenance metadata and SHA-256 checksums. In total, 44,171 connected LC classes and 437,212 graph/m pairs were checked. The classification contains 20 RESISTANT decisions, 437,192 FAIL decisions, and zero UNKNOWN decisions. The resistant Danielsen classes are: - N=5: m=0, ID 5; m=1, ID 8. - N=6: m=0, ID 9; m=2, IDs 16, 18, and 19. - N=7: m=0, ID 20. - N=8: m=0, ID 46; m=3, IDs 138 and 142. - N=9: m=0, ID 147. - N=10: m=0, ID 587; m=4, IDs 3174, 3175, 3498, 3636, 3668, 3699, and 3701. - N=11: m=0, ID 3719. No other resistant classes were found. In particular, all 40,457 connected N=11 LC classes were checked for m=0,...,9. The only resistant N=11 representative is the m=0 class with Danielsen ID 3719, represented by the 11-vertex star; no N=11 class is resistant for m≥1. This version extends the earlier deposited materials by adding the complete N=11 classification and a consolidated, self-contained reproduction program. The Danielsen representatives originate from the Database of Entanglement in Graph States. Exact source URLs, citations, class counts, and source-file hashes are recorded in data/source_metadata.json.

summary: Overview This repository contains the two processed datasets analyzed in "Influence of land cover and shade on the thermal environments of schoolyards in Los Angeles" by Levinson et al. (in preparation). The data come from the LAUSD Cool Schoolyards experiment, a field study of how schoolyard surfaces affect surface temperature, air temperature, radiant heat, and outdoor thermal comfort at Los Angeles Unified School District (LAUSD) elementary schools. The study compares four surface types: uncoated asphalt pavement, pavement with a high-reflectance coating (coated pavement), turf, and garden. The first file holds mobile measurements taken with an instrumented cart that was moved across each schoolyard. The second holds continuous measurements from three stationary weather stations placed over different surfaces. Study sites and measurement periods Each school is identified in the data by a two-letter code: HE : Harrison Elementary School, City Terrace, Los Angeles, CA BE : Braddock Drive Elementary School and Gifted Magnet, Culver City area, Los Angeles, CA SE : Saticoy Elementary School, North Hollywood, Los Angeles, CA Mobile cart measurements were made at HE on 2025-09-06, at BE on 2025-09-07, and at SE on 2025-09-14. The weather stations were deployed at BE from 2025-09-10 13:00 to 2025-10-10 09:00 and at HE from 2025-10-10 14:00 to 2025-11-02 00:00. File 1: Transect measurements Transect measurement stats at 1 min + coded transects + open-meteo weather + shade + LSH.csv An instrumented cart was moved along a route of numbered locations ("transect points") across each schoolyard. At each point it stopped for about one minute and recorded readings every second. Each row summarizes one stop, giving the mean, standard deviation, minimum, and maximum of every measured variable. The route was traversed repeatedly in forward and reverse directions. The file includes: Identifiers: school, measurement number, transect point, a tag of the form MMM_SS_PP (measurement number, school, point), transect number, and direction. Microclimate: air temperature, relative humidity, and wind speed and direction measured about 1.5 m above the ground. Radiation and surfaces: downward solar irradiance, ground albedo (the fraction of sunlight the ground reflects), ground surface temperature, sky temperature, and mean radiant temperature (MRT, a measure of the total radiant heat a person receives). Readings from 12 radiometers are also included: six measuring sunlight and six measuring longwave (thermal) radiation, facing up, down, forward, back, left, and right. Instrument orientation and position: radiometer tilt, roll, and zenith angles, plus GPS coordinates. Surface properties: surface description and classification of each point, along with measured solar reflectance and thermal emittance. Derived quantities: solar position, local solar hour, the Universal Thermal Climate Index (UTCI, an index of how hot conditions feel to a person) and its heat-stress category, and a shade classification for each stop. In the Classification column, the labels "Warm pavement," "Cool pavement," "Grass," and "Nature area" correspond to uncoated pavement, coated pavement, turf, and garden, respectively. summary: Fisher information metric tensors for the 41 held-out SONICOM test subjects, as used in “Evaluating Spatial Discriminability Preservation in HRTF Upsampling Using Fisher Information” (D. Bassett). Code and reproduction instructions: https://github.com/domfrbassett/fisher-rao-hrtf-upsampling What the tensors are At each of the 793 directions of the SONICOM grid, the 2×2 tensor g = JᵀΣ⁻¹J describes how well the auditory cues separate that direction from its neighbours. J is the spatial Jacobian of the cues: Barumerli monaural PGE features, ILD and MaxIACCe-transformed ITD, each fitted with real spherical harmonics. Σ holds the cue noise (σ_mon = 1.25 dB, σ_ILD = 1 dB, σ_ITD = 0.569). All fields are low-pass filtered at 16 kHz before the cues are extracted. The tensor is expressed in a local tangent basis u₁ = a × r, u₂ = r × u₁, where a = z, or y when |r_z| > 0.9, and its units are d′² per rad². Contents metric_tensors.zip has one folder per subject, metric_tensors/subject_####/ , containing 25 files per subject (1,025 in total): reference_metric_tensor.mat : the dense measured HRTF. <METHOD>_N###_metric_tensor.mat : one file per reconstruction. There are six methods: SUpDEq_SH , SUpDEq_MCA , SUpDEq_NN_MCA_6dB (SUpDEq-Natural-MCA in the paper), SUpDEq_Bary_MCA_6dB , RANF and FSP_AE . Each is reconstructed from N = 100, 19, 5 and 3 retained directions. The 164 natural-neighbour and barycentric files at N = 5 and 3 have status “ not_applicable ”. The interpolation is undefined for those masks, so these files carry no tensors. Variables in each file: metricTensor : the tensors at SH order 6 [2×2×793]. familyGram : per-cue-family Gram matrices JᵀJ before noise weighting, at SH orders 4, 6 and 8 [2×2×793×3 families×3 orders]. They let you recompute the tensors with other noise values or SH orders. In reconstruction files only: crossFamilyGram : the unsymmetrised cross terms J_refᵀ J_recon, same layout as familyGram . airmByDirection : the pointwise AIRM discrepancy from the reference. Metadata: coordinates (Cartesian and azimuth/elevation in degrees), cue band, noise values (reference files only), status (“ completed ” or “ not_applicable ”) and, for not-applicable files, a message giving the reason. SHA256SUMS.txt lists a checksum for every file. Format and use The files are MATLAB v7.3 (HDF5), so MATLAB, h5py or any HDF5 reader can open them. Note that h5py reverses MATLAB’s axis order. scripts/fisher_lib.py in the repository reads them and recomputes tensors, AIRM and thresholds from the Gram matrices. To rerun the analysis scripts, unzip into results/evaluation/ so the subject folders sit in results/evaluation/metric_tensors/ . Provenance Produced with run_evaluation("tensors") from the repository above. The values are numerically identical to the tensor files behind results/evaluation/full_evaluation_summary.csv ; this run additionally stores the cross terms. The tensors are derived from the SONICOM HRTF Dataset (Engel et al., J. Audio Eng. Soc. 71(5), 2023, doi:10.17743/jaes.2022.0066). The SONICOM HRTFs are released under the MIT licence. This work develops research begun for the author’s B.Sc. dissertation at Birmingham City University.

SHA256SUMS.txt lists a checksum for every file. Format and use The files are MATLAB v7.3 (HDF5), so MATLAB, h5py or any HDF5 reader can open them. Note that h5py reverses MATLAB’s axis order. scripts/fisher_lib.py in the repository reads them and recomputes tensors, AIRM and thresholds from the Gram matrices. To rerun the analysis scripts, unzip into results/evaluation/ so the subject folders sit in results/evaluation/metric_tensors/ . Provenance Produced with run_evaluation("tensors") from the repository above. The values are numerically identical to the tensor files behind results/evaluation/full_evaluation_summary.csv ; this run additionally stores the cross terms. The tensors are derived from the SONICOM HRTF Dataset (Engel et al., J. Audio Eng. Soc. 71(5), 2023, doi:10.17743/jaes.2022.0066). The SONICOM HRTFs are released under the MIT licence. This work develops research begun for the author’s B.Sc. dissertation at Birmingham City University.

summary: Code, pre-registrations, generated model text and result files for the manuscript “How Much Text Reveals a Watermark? A Detection Law for Keyless Auditing of Language-Model Watermarks” (submitted to IEEE Transactions on Information Forensics and Security). The archive holds the five pre-registered experiments of the paper: P54 (synthetic text, Unigram watermark), P54b (real text from Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct with fixed-list and context-keyed watermarks and a SmolLM2-1.7B-Instruct reference), P54c (repeated queries with the key derived from the whole prompt), P54d/P54e (repeated queries with the key from the last h tokens, passive counting of watermarks that are unbiased over keys including SynthID-Text, and additional real-text analyses) and P54f (the word-counting audit repeated on Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct). Each experiment folder contains the pre-registration with its SHA-256 lock file written before the run (Turkish original and English translation), the analysis and generation scripts, the generated text, the result files and a result note. The folder manuscript_numbers contains the script that produces every number, table and figure of the manuscript from the result files, so that no number in the paper is typed by hand. README.md describes the layout, how to verify the lock files and how to reproduce the numbers and the experiments; SHA256SUMS.txt lists the checksum of every file. Code: MIT licence. Text, pre-registrations and generated model outputs: CC BY 4.0. The generated texts are outputs of Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, SmolLM2-1.7B-Instruct and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct under their respective licences.

summary: We investigate the rigidity of smooth stationary solutions to the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations in ℝⁿ with singularities along a linear subspace Σ ≅ ℝᵏ. Assuming the scale-invariant transverse bound ‖u(x)‖ ≤ C‖x′‖⁻¹, where x′ ∈ ℝᵐ represents the transverse coordinates and m = n − k is the codimension of the singularity, we prove that u ≡ 0 provided m ≥ 4 and 1 ≤ k < m. This result generalizes the recent theorem of Gui, Liu, Wang, and Xie (2026), which corresponds to the case k = 1 and n ≥ 5. Our proof relies on a quantitative local regularity theorem showing that the transverse bound implies the removability of the singularity along Σ. The argument combines weak extension across the subspace, approximate Green functions for the adjoint drift operator, a one-sided bound for the total head pressure, and a localized Frehse–Růžička weighted estimate followed by a finite Stokes–Morrey bootstrap. Furthermore, we establish the sharpness of the codimension threshold m ≥ 4 by constructing non-trivial counterexamples for m = 1, m = 2, and m = 3 via trivial extensions of Jeffery–Hamel and Landau solutions, together with a new explicit family of non-trivial solutions in the borderline case m = 1. Finally, we discuss the technical obstruction preventing the immediate removal of the condition k < m and propose a conditional rigidity result under additional integrability assumptions.

summary: Abnormal  uterine  bleeding  (AUB)  is  a  symptom  rather  than  a  single disease, and diagnostic failure may follow when the bleeding phenotype is  mistaken for an etiological diagnosis. The International Federation of Gynecology  Obstetrics (FIGO) PALM–COEIN system provides a common vocabulary for  structural  and  nonstructural  causes,  but  its  practical  diagno stic  value  depends  on  examination  strategy,  phenotype  documentation,  access  to  investigations,  and  competing  risks.  Objective:  To  critically  evaluate  the  role  of  PALM–COEIN  in  triage, etiological work-up, longitudinal care, and real-world evidence generation,  with particular attention to digital decision support and feasibility in Uzbekistan

summary: QMBL: Open Problems is a record book of the state of the art in quantum many-body simulation for problems with no exact ground-state energy. Scientists and AI systems should use the shared results to build on each other's work more efficiently and advance frontier science. This snapshot holds the launch target list (targets/v1.json, 153 instances frozen from QMBL v0.4.0; 152 are open today, as one has since been solved exactly), the entry format and its checks, and the maintainer's re-measurement flow; the verifier is quantum-many-body-leaderboard/verifier.

summary: Underwater acoustic target detection and recognition are essential to marine surveillance and intelligent ocean sensing. Despite substantial advances in deep learning, existing systems typically produce binary detection decisions, categorical labels, or scalar confidence scores, offering limited insight into the physical evidence underlying their outputs. Large language models (LLMs) offer an opportunity to move underwater acoustic sensing toward interpretable, evidence-grounded understanding; however, generic audio encoders struggle to capture the distinctive physical characteristics of underwater acoustics, and physically annotated data are scarce. In this paper, the first of a two-part series, we propose a from-signals-to-evidence framework that integrates physics-aware acoustic encoding with a pretrained LLM, organized around a unified feature-evidence-decision chain with a shared reasoning core. An open input layer accommodates heterogeneous information-raw waveforms, time-frequency representations, environmental and geographic data, and textual physical priors-unifying detection and recognition within a common formulation. In Part I, we instantiate this framework for target recognition through an Underwater Acoustic Physics-aware Transformer (UPT), which tokenizes complementary acoustic representations and learns task-disentangled physical representations through four physics-oriented learning tasks. We develop a physics-parameterized data engine that provides traceable supervision at two levels of granularity and introduce an attribute-level evaluation protocol to assess the physical fidelity of generated descriptions. Experiments on simulated recordings of four vessels demonstrate accurate vessel recognition and reliable estimation of shaft frequency, blade-passing frequency, and machinery-related attributes.
title: From Signals to Evidence: Interpretable Underwater Acoustic Target Sensing with Large Language Models - Part I: Framework and Recognition

summary: Recent advances in deep learning have significantly improved underwater acoustic vessel recognition. However, existing publicly available datasets are typically limited in scale, hindering large-scale representation learning and downstream task evaluation. To address this limitation, we introduce ONCship, a large-scale underwater acoustic dataset comprising 4521 hours of curated recordings from Ocean Networks Canada (ONC) hydrophones and Automatic Identification System (AIS) data. We evaluate the proposed dataset across three tasks: self-supervised representation learning, vessel-type classification, and MMSI-Level Vessel Classification. Experiments on DeepShip and ShipsEar demonstrate the effectiveness of ONCship for acoustic representation learning, with joint pre-training on ONCship and AudioSet achieving a classification accuracy of 62.45% on DeepShip through linear probing. Furthermore, incorporating ONCship as auxiliary training data improves downstream vessel-type classification performance. Beyond conventional vessel-type classification, we further investigate MMSI-Level Vessel Classification, treating each vessel as a distinct identity. Experimental results show that models fine-tuned with different loss functions achieve Top-1 accuracies exceeding 53% and Top-5 accuracies approaching 69%, demonstrating the feasibility of distinguishing individual vessels through MMSI-Level Vessel Classification. Overall, ONCship provides a valuable resource for underwater acoustic representation learning and vessel recognition, while its rich vessel-level metadata enables further exploration of MMSI-Level Vessel Classification.
title: ONCship: A Large-Scale Underwater Acoustic Corpus for Ship Recognition

summary: Large audio-language models (LALMs) are fast becoming a general interface to sound, yet how far their broad pretraining carries into specialized domains remains largely open. Vessel monitoring, maritime safety, and ocean sensing all depend on recognizing underwater signals, but to our knowledge LALMs have not been systematically evaluated on them. Annotated recordings are costly to collect, and a faithful synthetic alternative has to bring together many interacting factors: the structure of detection pulses, communication waveforms, and ship-radiated noise, and the sound-speed profile, geometry, and multipath propagation through which each reaches the receiver. We address this by proposing \textbf{UA-Bench}, to our knowledge the first large-scale benchmark for evaluating LALMs on underwater acoustic signal recognition. It comprises 375,051 audio records that couple parameterized sources with modeled propagation, so that every record can be traced to the conditions that produced it. The records span these three signal families, and each carries a three-level label hierarchy (13 leaf classes), a templated multi-turn dialogue, and source and channel metadata. We evaluate on a balanced 2,600-record subset with a gated coarse-to-fine protocol that locates each error at source routing, fine-grained classification, or output format, and add a paired silent-audio control to test whether the waveform is actually used. Nine open LALMs, evaluated without task-specific adaptation, reach only 2.0\%--13.1\% leaf accuracy, against a random reference of 7.7\%. The waveform helps source routing far more than leaf recognition (for one model, +29.5 versus +2.3 points over silence), and just four models gain reliably at the leaf level, by at most 4.7 points. UA-Bench thus gives a reference point for these models, and its released training partition supports follow-up adaptation work.
title: UA-Bench: Benchmarking Large Audio-Language Models on Underwater Acoustic Recognition

We address this by proposing \textbf{UA-Bench}, to our knowledge the first large-scale benchmark for evaluating LALMs on underwater acoustic signal recognition. It comprises 375,051 audio records that couple parameterized sources with modeled propagation, so that every record can be traced to the conditions that produced it. The records span these three signal families, and each carries a three-level label hierarchy (13 leaf classes), a templated multi-turn dialogue, and source and channel metadata. We evaluate on a balanced 2,600-record subset with a gated coarse-to-fine protocol that locates each error at source routing, fine-grained classification, or output format, and add a paired silent-audio control to test whether the waveform is actually used. Nine open LALMs, evaluated without task-specific adaptation, reach only 2.0\%--13.1\% leaf accuracy, against a random reference of 7.7\%. The waveform helps source routing far more than leaf recognition (for one model, +29.5 versus +2.3 points over silence), and just four models gain reliably at the leaf level, by at most 4.7 points. UA-Bench thus gives a reference point for these models, and its released training partition supports follow-up adaptation work.
title: UA-Bench: Benchmarking Large Audio-Language Models on Underwater Acoustic Recognition

summary: Adaptive modulation and coding (AMC) improves the spectral efficiency of underwater acoustic (UWA) links, but its feedback is inevitably stale: sound propagates slowly, and by the time channel state information (CSI) arrives, the fast time-varying multipath channel has moved on. Predictive link adaptation therefore needs more than a point forecast: it needs a distribution over each candidate action's consequences. We propose PRB-WM, a physics-regularized Beta world model for predictive per-subcarrier link adaptation on real time-varying UWA channels. A persistence-anchored stochastic latent-space dynamics model learns how the channel evolves; a counterfactual outcome head evaluates, for every candidate modulation and coding scheme (MCS), a Beta-binomial distribution of bit errors on shared imagined futures; and a chance-constrained receding-horizon model predictive controller maximizes expected spectral efficiency subject to a bounded probability of violating the bit error rate (BER) target. To the best of our knowledge, PRB-WM is the first world model for UWA communications. In closed-loop replay of six measured sea-trial links from the public UWA Channel Library against a 24-method pool spanning the full methodological spectrum, PRB-WM attains a mean goodput 87% above the strongest baseline, ranks first on all six time-varying links at the longest lookahead, and is the only method whose realized frame risk decreases systematically with lookahead, meeting the BER-violation contract where no baseline does. Ablations confirm that rollout sampling dispersion is essential to the chance constraint and that the physics anchor is necessary for trainability.

summary: The underwater sound speed distribution directly governs acoustic propagation paths, rendering it critically important for underwater acoustic communication and target localization. Conventional sound speed profile (SSP) prediction methods provide a good way to estimate the underwater sound speed distribution without on-site data measurement, thus breaking through the coverage area constraints of sonar observation equipment and making the model universal in most marine areas. However, underwater sound speed exhibits multi-scale variations, such as diurnal, quarterly, and intermittent fluctuations caused by ocean processes such as internal waves. This makes it difficult for the fixed structure models in existing methods to have good generalization ability for multi-scale sound speed distribution patterns. To tackle this problem, we proposed a lightweight hybrid basis-function empowered Kolmogorov-Arnold network (LHBF-KAN) model for multi-scale sound speed prediction. We aim to construct a multi-branch representation layer in which different basis functions respond to distinct temporal patterns, from slowly varying background trends to rapid fluctuations induced by dynamic ocean processes, allowing the model to naturally accommodate the inherently multi-scale evolution of sound speed at different depths. To prevent the multi-branch structure from increasing model size, a pruning strategy is further introduced to suppress branches with consistently low contribution during training, yielding a compact architecture, suitable for deployment on resource constrained underwater platforms.
title: Robust Prediction of Internal Wave-Affected Multi-Scale Sound Speed Distribution Using Lightweight Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks with Hybrid Basis Functions

summary: Ultrasound (US)-based auricular vagus nerve stimulation (aVNS) is emerging as a versatile, noninvasive modality for neuromodulation - spanning clinical therapies (e.g., pain management, depression) and general well-being applications. However, most existing US-based aVNS systems remain bulky and require wet coupling media (e.g., ultrasound gel) to achieve both spatially localized stimulation and efficient acoustic transmission. We present a wearable US stimulation system combining a personalized, dry-coupled earpiece with a battery-powered, wireless US probe. The earpiece integrates a 2 MHz piezoelectric transducer fully encapsulated in Humimic material designed for anatomical fit and stable coupling without externally applied gel. Hydrophone measurements of the fully encapsulated earpiece in water give a peak rarefactional pressure of 0.24 MPa at 15 mm for a 15 V unipolar excitation. We further demonstrate in vivo feasibility through fully dry, in-ear 2 MHz pulse-echo acquisitions under realistic wearing conditions, confirming effective US transmission without the need for coupling gel. These results demonstrate the integration of a personalized dry acoustic interface with battery-powered stimulation electronics, providing a wearable platform for investigating US-based aVNS. Future studies will focus on functional outcomes, including heart rate variability and pupillary responses during stimulation.
title: Towards an Earpiece for Wearable and Dry Ultrasonic Vagus Nerve Stimulation

summary: Localizing an autonomous underwater vehicle without pre-deployed seabed transponders, or direct access to onboard vehicle sensors remains a core challenge. We present a receiver-passive 3-D localization and spatial mapping system utilizing a single floating surface buoy equipped with a hydrophone array and an inertial measurement unit (IMU). The central difficulty is that surface wave motion induces six-degree-of-freedom (6-DOF) perturbations that rotate the array between snapshots, degrading conventional subspace processing. We resolve this by introducing a fixed-point iterative MUltiple SIgnal Classification algorithm (FP-MUSIC) that uses IMU measurements to de-warp snapshot covariances prior to direction-of-arrival estimation. Furthermore, we employ a subspace-projected wideband matched filter to resolve beacon ranges and use power asymmetry for independent front-back identification. Evaluations across simulated sea states demonstrate that FP-MUSIC substantially reduces localization error relative to uncompensated methods and sustains robust 3-D tracking and vehicle orientation estimation under wave-induced motion. At moderate sea state, FP-MUSIC increases the 2-m beacon-separation accuracy from approximately 45% to 75%.
title: Wave-Robust Passive AUV Localization Using FP-MUSIC

We resolve this by introducing a fixed-point iterative MUltiple SIgnal Classification algorithm (FP-MUSIC) that uses IMU measurements to de-warp snapshot covariances prior to direction-of-arrival estimation. Furthermore, we employ a subspace-projected wideband matched filter to resolve beacon ranges and use power asymmetry for independent front-back identification. Evaluations across simulated sea states demonstrate that FP-MUSIC substantially reduces localization error relative to uncompensated methods and sustains robust 3-D tracking and vehicle orientation estimation under wave-induced motion. At moderate sea state, FP-MUSIC increases the 2-m beacon-separation accuracy from approximately 45% to 75%.

Linux Professional Institute®: LPIC-1. LPIC-2. LPIC-3*. Linux Foundation®: Linux Foundation Certified IT Associate (LFCA). Linux Foundation Certified System Administrator (LFCS).    The book covers the following chapters (in summary): Open source licenses and philosophy, open source software & license comparison. What are the advantages of Linux and open source software. Linux distributions and distribution types. Principles of operating systems: basic mechanisms and way of working of operating systems. System administration: Work with user accounts and groups. System security configuration (file permissions, timestamps, ACL, SELinux ). Service management (installation, configuration, ...) Software/package management: Patch management Archiving and backup. Process management. Computer components and optimizations: Motherboard and chipset. Block devices and partitioning, disk formats, and filesystems. RAID (hardware and software) and LVM2 NAS and SAN storage systems overview SAN storage systems: iSCSI Fibre Channel (FC) Disk I/O subsystems and optimizations. Disk I/O performance and monitoring  System analysis and optimizations (perf, strace, ltrace, dstat). Working with log files and services. Kernel dump/core dump. Computer networks: Copper vs Optical networks: Copper: cabling and standards. Fiberoptics: standards, cabling, FTTH specifics. Network interfaces (NIC) design and details, classic (copper) NICs (RJ-45), and SFP specifics. Networking concepts and protocols (topology, CSMA/CD, Bridging, OSI model): OSI 2 model and protocols: Bridges, ARP, and Flow control. STP, LACP, LLDP, OSI 2 network interfaces,.... OSI 3 model and protocols: IP, QoS, IP Fragmentation. TTL, MTU. NAT (DNAT, SNAT). Redundancy and VRRP, .... Transport layer: UDP  TCP: SYN, ACK, SACK.  TCP Window, Window scaling, congestion control.  PSH&URG, ... . Multipath TCP Network in Linux (configuration and details). Optimizing network interfaces and services for 10+Gbps (10/25/100Gbps) Common network commands:  traceroute, nslookup. netstat, nstat, ss, lsof. ip, ethtool. tcpdump. Network services and protocols: DHCP, Bootp, TFTP DNS: Protocol details Types of DNS requests DNS records: A, AAA, PTR, CNAME, DNAME, MX, NS, SOA, SPF, DKIM, DMARC, ... Telnet and SSH. NFS E-mail: SMTP, POP3, IMAP HTTP/HTTPS, Proxy NTP Syslog SNMP Work with the firewall: iptables ipset nftables eBPF Namespaces and isolation Virtualization and Linux containers: LXC  Podman Security: Enforcements Compliance (NIST, CIS, DISA STIG, ...) Many extras: list of Linux commands, list of terms, list of important files, interface bandwidth, ... Advanced and expert chapters as an addition to all the mentioned chapters and units.
